title: ‘Just an easy cash grab’: why Jetstar is charging customers for carry-on luggage
summary:
Add-on fees such as the new overhead locker baggage charge can make it harder to compare air fares, experts say

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Cut-price fares may now be merely a facade for seemingly endless add-on fees after Jetstar’s new carry-on luggage charge meant the airline joined a growing number monetising basic services in the sky.

The new structure, announced by Qantas’s low-cost carrier on Wednesday, will mean from next year tickets will only include one “under seat bag”, such as a backpack, handbag or laptop bag.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Cut-price fares may now be merely a facade for seemingly endless add-on fees after Jetstar’s new carry-on luggage charge meant the airline joined a growing number monetising basic services in the sky.
The new structure, announced by Qantas’s low-cost carrier on Wednesday, will mean from next year tickets will only include one “under seat bag”, such as a backpack, handbag or laptop bag.
Customers with stowed carry-on luggage will face an additional layer of fees, building on costs for check-in baggage, preferred seats, cancellation rights and meals and snacks.
It is the latest pricing change in a sector where multiple airlines now even give passengers an option to pay to be next to a vacant seat, in a clever strategy that allows carriers to charge for tickets that do not otherwise sell.
In an extreme example of pricing changes, Canadian airline WestJet reconfigured its aircraft last year, requiring passengers to pay an extra fee if they wanted a seat that reclines.
Such changes are usually marketed by the airlines as a simplified, user-pay system that keeps entry level prices low for those looking for a cheap fare.
But Graeme Hughes, a consumer expert and adjunct associate professor at Griffith University, says it further obscures the checkout price.
“This allows Jetstar to broadcast the cheapest price, but of course those add-on costs are something which are going to hit you as you click through the booking process,” Hughes says.
“There will be frustration there for travellers because it means they can’t easily do an apple-for-apple comparison with other airfares.”
Andy Kelly, the campaigns director at the consumer advocacy group Choice, says Jetstar’s new policy is “just an easy cash grab, really”.
“Already, to choose seats could be over $20, around $50 if you want the ability to cancel your flight to get a credit, and then an additional $50 to join their loyalty program to get a discount,” he says.
“They just make it really hard for consumers to make an assessment of value and also to compare different products.”
European experience
The EU recently mandated that airlines – along with booking platforms and search engines – will have to display air fares that are inclusive of carry-on luggage at the outset of the booking process, to make it easier for consumers to compare prices.
The European Council introduced the mandate after fierce pushback from the airlines to an earlier proposal by the European parliament to give passengers the right to carry on a small case for free, as well as the free under seat bags currently permitted.
In its press release, Jetstar said its shift to a “size-based carry-on baggage model” was similar to other low-fare carriers around the world.
Jetstar also claimed the model helps keep fares low because “you only pay for what you need”.
Jetstar has tried to present the change as a positive development for travellers, but it is also following the lead of these overseas carriers in charging people to bring anything other than a small bag or item that can fit under the seat in front of them.
Dr Ian Douglas, an honorary senior lecturer at the University of New South Wales’ School of Aviation, says pretty much every low-cost carrier in Europe charges some sort of fee, including Ryanair and EasyJet.
“It’s a little sad we’ve gone straight to the Ryanair model because Jetstar is not Ryanair,” he says. “Jetstar is filling a gap in the Qantas network.
“If you want to go to the Sunshine Coast or Cairns [for example], it’s quite likely the offer will be Jetstar and not Qantas.”
Jetstar says the new fee will depend on the length of the flight and has acknowledged that fees may change. It can exceed $100 to carry an overhead bag on an overseas trip, according to Guardian Australia analysis of different Jetstar routes.
Ireland-headquartered Ryanair charges passengers €/£12-€/£36 if they pay when booking, or €/£20-€/£60 if they pay at the airport.
Britain’s EasyJet says its fees vary, including based on demand. Passengers who don’t pay in advance are charged £60 at the boarding gate.
The German low-cost carrier Eurowings charges basic-fare customers fees from €18 or £16 for “large” carry-on luggage.
In the US, leading low-cost carriers JetBlue and Southwest include a small personal item and a larger carry-on bag in their fares, while Frontier charges passengers based on their route.

title: The events at Ceuta ​show ​how Europe’s ​hard ​right ​now ​set the ​tone​ on immigration
summary:
The narratives of the right are seeping into mainstream EU policy, and Spain finds itself increasingly isolated in its humanitarian stance on borders

• Don’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

It was over almost as quickly as it began. But the human cost of the mayhem in Ceuta over the last seven days, and the disunity it exposed within the EU, will take a lot longer to fix.

To recap: more than 70,000 people swam or waded into the tiny Spanish enclave in north Africa from neighbouring Morocco in a matter of hours at the end of last week. The exact circumstances in which the heavily securitised border came suddenly to be open are still unclear.

Continue reading...
full_text:
It was over almost as quickly as it began. But the human cost of the mayhem in Ceuta over the last seven days, and the disunity it exposed within the EU, will take a lot longer to fix.
To recap: more than 70,000 people swam or waded into the tiny Spanish enclave in north Africa from neighbouring Morocco in a matter of hours at the end of last week. The exact circumstances in which the heavily securitised border came suddenly to be open are still unclear.
What is clear is that at least 88 people died. Some drowned, others were trampled in the crush. Social media hyped a distorted version of events. Far-right parties, already driving the agenda on migration across Europe, weaponised the story. And Spain’s EU allies engaged in a war of words – not over the plight of those caught up in the tragedy, but over who let them into EU territory.
Italy and Denmark jointly led the way there, accusing Madrid of failing to secure the EU’s only land border with Africa. Although Ceuta is not even in the EU’s Schengen passport-free travel area, Giorgia Meloni, the far-right Italian prime minister, performatively suspended Schengen rights for travellers entering Italy from Spain.
Meloni and her Danish counterpart, Mette Frederiksen (although a Social Democrat, is another migration hardliner), wrote to the EU demanding emergency talks on tightening the bloc’s external borders. They enlisted the backing of all but five of the 27 EU leaders.
Faced with such an unusual lack of support, Spain’s Pedro Sánchez could only protest about the “selfish, polarising and unlawful” response of his EU allies.
By Monday the vast majority who arrived in Ceuta had gone back to Morocco. None attempted to reach the Spanish mainland or to abscond towards any other country’s borders. Of those left stranded on the streets of the city, many were unaccompanied children.
By then, Donald Trump, Elon Musk and Israeli ministers had weighed in to decry Europe’s “migrant invasion”, and Ceuta had begun to function, wrote Jonathan Liew, “as a kind of border porn for the global far right: a locus upon which to project their most vivid and apocalyptic fantasies”. The spectacle of left-liberal Spain facing a migration crisis of its own making was, for the European hard right and the White House “almost too good to be true”, Ruben Andersson wrote.
But why the frenzy among European governments? Paul Taylor, a senior fellow with the European Policy Centre, says there was a shamelessly cynical interest for some EU leaders to pile on and isolate Madrid. The reaction was very different in the past, when Poland and Lithuania faced migrant incursions weaponised by Belarus.
“Most EU governments are conservative or rightwing-led and have an interest in scapegoating Spain, which is governed by a socialist-leftist coalition, and in helping Spain’s rightwing opposition ahead of a general election due next year, and in trying to win back voters in their own countries who are defecting to rightwing populists,” Taylor said.
Within the EU, Sanchez has swum against the tide, standing up to the Trump administration over Gaza, the war in Iran and Nato defence spending. During the recent wildfires he was vocal about climate backsliding. In an EU where policy has been hardening since 2015, he bucks the trend on migration, too.
“Spain has been an outlier, welcoming migration and actively working to integrate migrants into the economy and society,” Taylor said. “This is seen as an affront by many conservative politicians but also as a ‘pull factor’ encouraging would-be migrants to try their luck in Europe at a time when official EU policy is to combat irregular migration, crack down on abuses of the asylum system and park asylum seekers offshore in countries outside the bloc.”
And this is exactly the bigger political bone Meloni, Frederiksen and others wanted to pick with Spain. In their letter to the EU, ostensibly about the immediate crisis in Ceuta, they targeted Madrid’s recent policy of allowing undocumented people working in mainland Spain to regularise their migration status, even though this was irrelevant for those involved in the Ceuta situation.
What is most striking about this, Taylor said, is the hypocrisy and double standards of Spain’s critics.
“Many of those criticising Spain’s amnesty allowing irregular migrants to apply for residence permits have introduced similar schemes in their own countries. Italy and Germany have both given work permits and/or the right to remain to irregular migrants already working there in programmes supported by employers plagued by labour shortages.”
Why Ceuta? Why now?
What actually provoked the Ceuta surge remains unexplained.
One theory is that misleading posts circulated on Instagram, TikTok and Facebook following a 29 June Spanish supreme court ruling that clarified that under international law, the state cannot summarily deport migrants who arrive by sea without due process.
But many suspect geopolitical mischief by Morocco – possibly to extract payback for Spain’s recent detente with its regional rival Algeria. If this is the case then the EU’s controversial strategy of outsourcing migration to regimes such as Morocco’s, looks even more problematic. Ashifa Kassam recalled in this Guardian podcast how Morocco weaponised migrants in a previous incident in 2021, allowing 10,000 people to cross into Ceuta during a diplomatic standoff with Spain over Western Sahara.
By Tuesday, EU justice and home affairs ministers were publicly papering over their split, although Brussels criticised Spain’s amnesty for undocumented migrants as “not a good signal for the rest of Europe”.
Ministers endorsed a plan to strengthen Europe’s external borders, including an early warning system and better “cooperation” with non-EU countries on migration: possibly code for more “cash for migration” deals with often unsavoury regimes.
The Ceuta episode could also lead to the acceleration of ICE-style deportations from the EU. The Italian government in particular wants to see offshore migration centres, or “return hubs”, made possible under the EU’s new return regulation.
Yet in a Europe devoid of safe and legal routes for asylum seekers, this is a direction that some of the most senior European legal experts have warned could create a “human rights black hole”.
When the European parliament voted to approve the return regulation last month, there was some dismay as far-right and rightwing MEPs celebrated in the chamber with raucous chants of “send them back!” On the evidence of the last week, it seems that Europe’s mainstream leaders have normalised the same chilling sentiment.

title: Ryan Murphy’s Teen Serial Killer Thriller The Shards Gets Stuck in the Shallow End
summary: Ryan Murphy and Bret Easton Ellis' FX adaptation of Ellis' '80s teen serial killer novel never grasps the poignancy it's reaching for
full_text:
A fruitful collaboration between Ryan Murphy and Bret Easton Ellis sounds, at once, inevitable and impossible. Murphy is a maximalist in every sense—a superproducer pumping out show after operatic show, writing characters who say the quiet part of every story out loud—and one of TV’s most influential promoters of inclusive, identity-politics-driven programming. Ellis, for his part, is known for the minimalistic prose of his generation-defining debut novel, Less Than Zero, and a more recent culture-warrior phase in which he has inveighed against the same “fake-woke corporate culture” within the entertainment industry that some might say Murphy epitomizes. On the other hand, both men are inveterate provocateurs, unafraid to alienate audiences and fascinated by the psychology of psycho killers (see: Ellis’ American Psycho and a huge chunk of Murphy’s output) and the interplay between pop culture and real life. Born on the boomer-Generation X cusp, they also remember what it was like to grow up gay in the ’80s.
In The Shards, which the two adapted from Ellis’ 2023 novel, the synergy among their experiences outweighs but doesn’t erase the irreconcilability of their perspectives. The story at its surface, an autofictional but otherwise familiar account of a serial killer stalking students at Ellis’ high school in 1981, gleams with the stylish production design, savvy genre pastiche, and elaborate set pieces for which Murphy is known. Yet it’s clear the show, premiering with two episodes on FX and Hulu on Aug. 5, has greater ambitions. In the connections it makes to cultural touchstones of its period and voiceover narration from a present-day Bret, The Shards attempts to say something profound about the transition from youth to adulthood. Blame a mismatched creative team or the visual medium’s inherent privileging of images over ideas; the shallow stuff wins out.
Like Less Than Zero—and in some ways a prequel to that novel, which took place during a college break, though Bret (played by an unnervingly self-possessed Igby Rigney) is also writing the book while this story unfolds—The Shards follows a clique of rich, debauched teens in L.A. Bret is noncommittally dating Debbie (rising pop star Hayes Warner), a ruthless go-getter, while secretly hooking up with guys. Their best friends are the class golden couple, gorgeous student body president Susan (Kaia Gerber), who wins every popularity contest even though she’d prefer not to, and Thom (Graham Campbell), an all-American dreamboat whose sadness no one perceives beneath an expression of what Bret calls “intriguing blankness.” Whether it’s the love Bret harbors for Susan or a fundamental lack of attraction to women in general that keeps him distant for Debbie is a question that lingers in the background as his identity crisis deepens.
Senior year is starting and the group’s parents have long since checked out. (Bret’s are apparently vacationing overseas.) Which suits the performatively jaded teens, who chain-smoke at restaurants with white tablecloths and traverse the city without curfew or constraint. Only Debbie’s monstrous family enters the frame. Her father, Terry (Wes Bentley), is a stock predatory movie producer with an eye for underage boys. His wife, Liz (Evan Rachel Wood), is a sneak preview of Debbie’s future, self-medicating with drugs, alcohol, and wrathful outbursts. The fourth member of the household is Terry’s lurking aide, an androgynous aesthete named Steven (theater producer Jordan Roth, playing up the character’s feline strangeness). When the situation calls for a responsible adult, these are not the people you want on hand.
They’re who the kids are stuck with, though, when a girl’s mangled body is found fastened to a tennis net and their classmates start disappearing. Bret is certain that the handsome new boy in school, Robert Mallory (Homer Gere), is the culprit. But his logic—that Robert must be a killer because he denies having been at the screening of The Shining where Bret first spotted him—is pretty flimsy. For some reason, Bret can’t get his friends to care about the murders. They’re too busy planning homecoming festivities and angling to get on dance-contest TV shows. Maybe their denial can be shrugged off as typical teen self-involvement, but it doesn’t explain why he seems more invested in the case than police and even some parents of the missing.
The Shards is dense with references. To make sense of the show beyond the plot’s generic teenage politicking and serial-killer thrills, you must know that The Shining is a horror story about a writer becoming violently unhinged; that its other Jack Nicholson footnote, Chinatown, is synonymous with systemic evil too entrenched to fight; that the financial disaster that was Michael Cimino’s 1980 feature Heaven’s Gate symbolizes the end of New Hollywood’s auteur-driven ’70s renaissance, leaving the industry to chase youthful faces and shiny trends. (Bret gives a Patrick-Bateman-esque monologue about how music videos are the future of art.) The casting piles new signifiers atop the source material. Gerber is the spookily identical daughter of Cindy Crawford, the ultimate Gen X beauty. Gere shares a square jaw with his father, Richard, whose breakthrough movie, American Gigolo—another tale of sex and murder in L.A., whose writer-director, Paul Schrader, worked with Ellis on The Canyons—was released just in time to be referenced by The Shards’ characters. Richard Gere was married to Crawford in the early ’90s. Gerber and Homer Gere don’t share any parents, but the connection adds a pseudo-incestuous twinge to their characters’ mutual attraction. Dig deeper, and you’ll find that Homer Gere’s mother, the actor Carrie Lowell, was once married to Griffin Dunne, the nephew of Joan Didion, whose work both Ellis and his Shards alter ego idolize.
Because so much of the meaning here resides in allusions that will elude most viewers under 40, Murphy and Ellis have essentially made two shows in one—an arch teen murder soap in the vein of Riverdale-Pretty Little Liars, and something more layered and harder to pin down for the older crowd. While the former benefits from the sensory intensity of Murphy’s storytelling (The Shards’ swimming pools achieve the incandescent blueness of Donald Trump’s Reflecting Pool dreams), and Ellis’ influence seems to have reined in some of his co-creator’s usual excesses, only the latter feels like something new. Yet the more thoughtful elements remain at the margins. It’s intriguing when the narrator says, for instance, “Matt had never felt about me the way I felt about him, which would be a recurring theme for the rest of my life.” The older Bret’s wistfulness, his frustration with a precocious teen Bret who traded his childhood innocence for an adult author’s life before he’d developed the self-knowledge that comes with genuine maturity, peeks through the surface without quite penetrating it.
The Shards unravels in its final few episodes. One plays on the name of the crew’s hangout, Hamburger Hamlet, drawing Murphy-ish parallels between the characters and Shakespeare’s tragic personages that are so overwrought, they can’t be salvaged by self-awareness. The bigger disappointment is a bombshell ending, albeit a narratively ambiguous one, that fizzles rather than explodes. The psychological escalation that’s supposed to lead us there never fully happens. This show about the consequences of limited introspection suffers them as well.

title: The Winners and Losers From Michigan's High-Stakes Senate Primary
summary: What the tight outcome means for Abdul El-Sayed, AIPAC and Chuck Schumer
full_text:
The DC Brief
Twice A Week
Making sense of what matters most in Washington.
Abdul El-Sayed, a rabble-rousing populist and former public health official, just barely eked out a primary victory Tuesday in Michigan over a centrist rival who was the pick of Washington Democrats to keep a must-hold Senate seat. It was a bad night for the Democratic Establishment, who see the outcome as a major setback to their party's dreams of clawing back control of the Upper Chamber for the final two years of President Donald Trump’s presidency.
But El-Sayed’s squeaker win was not what he or his allies were forecasting as recently as Tuesday morning. For weeks, most polling indicated Michiganders were strongly trending toward El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim Senator if he prevails in November over former Rep. Mike Rogers. Even still, this outcome was not something many foresaw as recently as last year. El-Sayed managed to captured the broad, bipartisan frustration that established leaders are not hearing voters’ concerns.
Strategists are still looking at the data but some top-line folks clearly came out winners—and others losers.
WINNER: El-Sayed
Even if he fell short of expectations, the podcasting populist still had the primary outcome he was counting on. El-Sayed has been planning this moment for a while. He ran for Governor in 2018, another wave year for Democrats, but lost his primary to the current Governor, Gretchen Whitmer.
As TIME’s Nik Popli reported from Michigan earlier this summer, El-Sayed is using his do-over to run against both parties at the same time. He blasted the wealthy, lashed the corporations, and decried the whole system as rigged. In many ways, he was channeling a lefty version of Trump.
El-Sayed, whose surprising rise prompted state senator Mallory McMorrow to suspend her campaign before voting began, is on the cusp of being the latest avatar for the brand of progressive and populist politics promoted by supporters like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez or Sen. Bernie Sanders. That instant credibility may boost El-Sayed nationally, but risks turning off voters in Michigan, which is precisely what Rep. Haley Stevens warned of during her unsuccessful primary against El-Sayed.
LOSER: Stevens
She had almost every on-paper advantage: a seat in the House, proximity to donors and advocacy groups, a policy wonk’s eye, and an affable every-woman folksiness. But CVs don’t always translate to votes.
Stevens, a former campaign aide to Hillary Clinton and Obama, couldn’t translate her natural political instinct as an operative to convincing a statewide electorate that she deserved their votes. Sometimes, her comments seemed to wander. Her mind moved faster than her lips. And her critics—in not-so-subtly-gendered language—mocked her accent.
Her defeat Tuesday cuts short her time in public office. At least for now.
WINNERS: Populists
The frustrations with the status quo helped El-Sayed, for sure. But it also reflects the true sentiment of how Americans are feeling right now. According to Gallup polling, just 23% of Americans are satisfied with how things are going. With that level of angst, it’s little wonder that Michiganders opted to go with someone calling for remaking the whole system over an incrementalist and pragmatist who pitched herself as someone who can fix the system from the inside.
But, again, this result in Michigan may be a complicating factor as Democrats try to figure out their next leaders. The 2028 presidential primary is already shaping up as yet another soul-searching moment for Democrats, pitting the disparate ideological camps and competing personalities against each other. But winning primaries, even in swing states, doesn’t necessarily mean much when it comes to assembling a broader coalition. As one Democratic strategist told me before polls closed on Tuesday, the night “gives 2028-ers the wrong idea about everything.”
LOSER: AIPAC
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee became an unlikely flashpoint in Michigan. The pro-Israel group has been spending big for several cycles to support allies of Israel and counter increasingly anti-Israel sentiments in the Democratic Party. El-Sayed’s views there left little doubt which side AIPAC would be supporting.
The group spent a record $30 million to help Stevens, an outlay that fed El-Sayed’s characterization of his opponent as little more than a mouthpiece for her deep-pocketed supporters.
While the group is nominally focused on promoting the relationship between the United States and Israel, its advertising focus seldom mentions Israel. In fact, a New York Times analysis of AIPAC’s ads since April of 2022 found 109 ads. Just six mention Israel.
WINNER: CAIR
Michigan is home to one of the nation’s largest and most politically engaged Muslim communities. And one of its most important civic engagement groups, the Council on American-Islamic Relations, or CAIR, pulled a last-minute flex in the final hours of the race.
On the eve of Tuesday’s primary, CAIR began a robocall effort that reached more than 13,000 Muslim Michigan households, where roughly 29,000 mail-in ballot recipients are registered. Another 19,000 low-propensity Muslim voters got calls.
Given El-Sayed’s narrow win, that push looks even more impactful, allowing the country’s largest Muslim civil rights groups to more firmly showcase its power in Michigan, as it finds itself targeted on multiple fronts in some red states.
LOSERS: Establishment Democrats
Stevens was the undisputed choice of the Democratic Establishment. She was a swing state Democrat who previously won on the same ballot as Trump. She had been through the vetting, could raise money, and seemed a practical choice to hold the seat of retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.
But Washington insiders’ efforts to help Stevens actually worked against her in a year when Democratic voters were more aligned with El-Sayed’s contempt for the Establishment. That anger found a vessel in El-Sayed and a target in Stevens. Even though Democratic leaders didn't get their way, that doesn't mean they're giving up on Michigan. Quickly after El-Sayed's primary victory became clear, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair, released a statement of support. “We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November," they said.
ACTING LIKE WINNERS: Republicans
Senate Republicans have been rightly nervous about holding their narrow majority. El-Sayed’s nomination takes away some of that stress. While Michigan is expected to be a close race, Republicans were a lot more eager to run against El-Sayed than Stevens. Republicans are ready with plenty of fodder from El-Sayed’s past comments; his unrelenting criticism of Israel will be wielded to sway Michigan’s Jewish voters to either back Rogers or sit the race out.
LOSER: Whitmer
For the longest time, the state’s popular Governor insisted she was not getting involved in the primary. She had defeated El-Sayed to win the nomination in 2018 and has led a diverse state party through some tough family fights, especially when it came to the 2024 presidential race. Whitmer, who is term-limited and will leave office after November’s elections, is often mentioned as a 2028 contender. She has, with varying levels of intensity, said she is not chasing the nomination, but clearly isn’t ready to end her political career.
So it left a lot of watchers surprised when, on July 24, Whitmer endorsed Stevens. It was a move that another Michigan Democrat and oft-mentioned 2028 contender, Sen. Elissa Slotkin, did not make. Whitmer quickly became one of Stevens’ better surrogates, making the argument in a clearer way than the candidate herself did.
As the folks in Whitmer’s lane look around, they may be questioning if there is a lane for their likes heading into 2028, or if a principled stand for pragmatism is truly a non-starter.

title: Abdul El-Sayed Wins Michigan Senate Primary, Delivering Progressives a Major Battleground Victory
summary: It’s a narrow but major victory for the Democrats' insurgent progressive wing.
full_text:
Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official, narrowly defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary, delivering the party’s insurgent progressive wing a major victory in a contest that became a fierce referendum on whether Democrats need to move further left to fully harness plummeting support for President Donald Trump.
The Associated Press called the race early Wednesday for El-Sayed, ending one of the midterm’s most expensive and bitter primary races. With 99% of the votes counted, El-Sayed was leading by about 15,000 votes, out of nearly 1.5 million votes cast. Michigan is widely viewed as critical to Democrats’ effort to regain control of the chamber, and some party leaders and strategists view El-Sayed as less competitive against Mike Rogers, the former congressman who ran unopposed in the Republican primary.
The race between El-Sayed, 41, and Stevens, 43, had become a proxy fight over the Democratic Party’s future. El-Sayed, a non-practicing doctor who previously ran for governor, built his campaign around a sweeping progressive agenda, calling for Medicare for All, a 7% annual tax on the wealth of billionaires, and a broader effort to challenge what he described as an economic system tilted toward the wealthy and powerful. “Democrats really should be afraid of what I mean for their system of politics,” El-Sayed told TIME in a wide-ranging interview in late May. “When I say I’m coming for it, I’m coming for all of it.”
For progressives, El-Sayed’s victory amounts to a rejection of an establishment seen as overly cautious, too closely aligned with corporate interests and unwilling to challenge traditional power centers. Stevens represented a different path: a candidate with deep party ties, more traditional experience in government, and a message focused on growing American manufacturing.
The primary unfolded amid uncertainty and rising tensions, defined in large part by deep ideological differences over Israel, an issue in which younger and more progressive voters are increasingly more sympathetic with the Palestinian cause. El-Sayed sharply criticized Stevens over her support for continued military assistance to Israel and her refusal to call Israel’s actions in Gaza a genocide. He also hammered her on her relationship with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, whose aligned super PAC spent tens of millions supporting Stevens.
Stevens, a moderate from the Detroit suburbs elected to Congress in 2018, framed herself as the Democrat best positioned to keep the seat in Democratic hands, arguing that El-Sayed’s positions on Israel and other issues were out of step with the state’s electorate. On the campaign trail, she emphasized her record in Congress, her ties to Michigan’s manufacturing communities, and her experience working for former President Barack Obama during the auto industry bailout. “I’m the only candidate who can keep Michigan blue,” Stevens argued in the final days of the campaign.
Stevens called El-Sayed to concede Wednesday morning and vowed to back his candidacy. “This was a thorough and rigorous campaign that brought out the full span of views within the Democratic Party—and that is why we have primaries,” she said in a statement.
Senate control at stake
The stakes for Democrats were unusually high as they nominated a candidate to retain the seat being vacated by Sen. Gary Peters. The party faces a difficult Senate map and must defend vulnerable seats while attempting to gain ground elsewhere if they hope to win control of the chamber. Losing Michigan, strategists in both parties have argued, could make the path to a Democratic majority far more difficult.
That math puts Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer in a complicated position after he backed Stevens over El-Sayed, who had told TIME that he wanted to replace Schumer with progressive Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen. Soon after the race was called, Schumer and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand issued a statement of support for El-Sayed: “Democrats are united by a common purpose: putting a check on Donald Trump by defeating his Republican enablers and taking back the Senate. We look forward to working with Abdul and Democrats across Michigan to win this seat in November."
Republicans had quietly hoped that El-Sayed would emerge as the Democratic nominee, believing some of his progressive views could provide them an opening in a state that has repeatedly shifted between the parties. Conservative groups have spent months portraying him as too radical for Michigan, focusing on his policy positions, his criticism of Israel, and his association with the political commentator Hasan Piker. Piker has faced criticism for past comments, including remarks that America deserved the Sept. 11 attacks that he later said he regretted. On the eve of the primary, El-Sayed once again campaigned with Piker, which Republicans pointed to as evidence of a broader ideological extremism.
Trump celebrates
Trump, who has endorsed Rogers, celebrated El-Sayed’s win as “great news” for the Republican Party. “El-Sayed, a communist loser who hates Jews and Israel, is the projected winner in his race with the socialist,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
El-Sayed previously told TIME that he does not consider himself a socialist even though his backers include prominent members of the Democratic Socialists of America. “I have no fealty to a dead German guy in his writing,” he said. “I actually think that at the small and local scale, capitalism is a great way to allocate resources, as long as everybody has access to it.”
With the general election race now set, Michigan’s Muslim and Jewish communities are likely to draw intense interest in the coming weeks. El-Sayed would be the first Muslim Senator in American history. His past comments on Israel, which he argues is guilty of genocide, have drawn fierce backlash from some Jewish leaders in Michigan, particularly after he linked a March attack on a Detroit-area synagogue to broader debates over Israel’s actions in Gaza, while still condemning the violence itself.
El-Sayed entered the race with a national following but a complicated political history. A Rhodes Scholar and graduate of Columbia Medical School who pursued a career in public health rather than practicing medicine, he served as Wayne County’s health director and gained national attention during a 2018 campaign for governor of Michigan in which he lost in the Democratic primary. In the years since, he has written books, hosted a podcast, and become a prominent voice in progressive circles.
His win comes just weeks after several Democratic socialist and progressive candidates scored major primary upsets against long-term establishment incumbents in safe-blue districts. On Wednesday, Michigan Rep. Shri Thanedar became the latest example, losing his primary to democratic socialist Donovan McKinney.
The Senate race in Michigan shifted in early July when Democrat Mallory McMorrow, a state senator, dropped out of the primary, reconfiguring the contest as a direct confrontation between two sharply different visions of the party.
Stevens consolidated support from many establishment Democrats, including Schumer and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, while El-Sayed strengthened his alliance with progressives, campaigning alongside Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
In the final weeks, the race grew increasingly personal. El-Sayed accused Stevens of representing a failing political establishment and mocked the outside spending supporting her campaign. Stevens responded by accusing him of focusing more on national attention than on Michigan voters and warning that his approach would make it harder for Democrats to win in November.

title: What to Say to Someone Who Is Dying, According to Hospice Workers
summary: There’s no perfect script. Showing up matters more.
full_text:
Sydney Mishkin’s father had Stage IV sarcoma for seven years. In the weeks before he died, she kept trying to figure out what she still hadn’t told him. She searched through their old texts and listened to his voicemails. At night, she lay awake reviewing their entire relationship, desperate to identify the words she might one day regret leaving unsaid.
Eventually, she realized there weren’t any. A week before her father passed away, Mishkin told him: “There’s nothing I’ve ever wanted to say and didn’t.” He was very weak, but he managed to answer: “I could not ask for a better daughter.” Within days, he was no longer able to speak.
The exchange was deeply meaningful—but also bittersweet. Mishkin worried she had said too much or made her father feel obligated to summon the energy for a profound response. “How do you sum up a lifetime of loving somebody into a sentence or two?” she says.
The answer, according to people who spend their careers alongside the dying, is that you don’t have to. There are words that can bring comfort, invite honesty, and help both of you find peace. But there’s no perfect script—and your presence likely matters more than anything you manage to say.
Don't wait for the right moment
When people ask Dr. Ira Byock whether they should make the trip to see a seriously ill friend or relative, he answers with a question: “Would you go to the funeral?”
Almost always, they say yes—of course they would. "Well, go now,” says Byock, a palliative care physician in Montana and author of The Four Things That Matter Most. You'll say generous things at the memorial about what a remarkable person your friend was. Better to say them while she can hear you. "It's much more fun to say those nice things when somebody is alive," Byock says. If you can only make one trip, make it this one.
Hadley Vlahos, a hospice nurse and author of The In-Between: Unforgettable Encounters During Life's Final Moments, regularly hears from families who want her to alert them when the end is near. Her answer never changes. "You need to come right now," she says. "Everyone looks for this perfect time, and they always think that there's gonna be more time." In hospice, the opposite is true: Beginning care earlier leaves more time for meaningful conversations. "You don't want to wait until they're in a coma," she says.
The window for a real back-and-forth closes before most families expect it to. Start when the diagnosis arrives, says Dr. Kate Brazzale, chief medical officer of Empath Health, which operates Florida’s largest nonprofit hospice network. "Don't wait, because the person that's dying needs to be able to respond and speak," she says. "You need to get all those things out of the way. Towards the end, the person that's dying may not be able to speak, and it's not very fair to unload on them at that point."
Sometimes there's no window at all. Christine Davies, director of spiritual care at Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital, has been a hospital chaplain for more than 25 years. She’s present for expected deaths after long illnesses, as well as sudden ones. "We may not even have the opportunity to say these last words, and so we have to say them all of the time," she says. "Knowing no day is promised makes it all the more sacred."
Lead with the obvious—and then let them talk
Once you're in the room, you don't need to read from a prepared statement. But on the drive or flight over, Byock suggests, think about what's most obvious to you, and open with that: “It's really good to see you. I've been thinking about you so much. It's just so good to be with you.”
From there, say the thing you assume they already know. "I so value our relationship. You've been so important to me," Byock offers as an example. Then get specific, the way you might at a celebration of life—without going overboard. “You've always been there for me.” “You're one of the funniest people I've ever known.” “What a remarkable parent you've been.”
"Notice I'm just saying the most obvious things," he says. "If the person means enough for you to travel and see them, they are important to you. This is a time to say it out loud."
Then shift the focus to how they’re feeling. Byock's go-to: “How are you doing physically—but also, how are you doing within yourself?” "That phrase is one that we don't hear very often, but people tend to know what I'm asking," he says.
If their answer surprises you—or you don’t quite understand it—don’t rush to reassure them or claim to know how they feel. Brazzale suggests three words instead: “Help me understand.” Unlike “I know how you feel,” which few people can truthfully say to someone who is dying, the phrase invites them to share more. “It opens the door,” she says.
She also asks patients directly whether they're afraid—one of her most effective questions, though she notes it lands differently coming from a physician than from a daughter. What surfaces is rarely just fear of physical pain. It's fear of the unknown, of losing control, and of what their loved ones will have to endure.
The conversation can also turn toward the past. Davies uses an approach called life review, inviting people to reflect on the experiences that shaped a person’s life—the highs and lows, regrets and celebrations, important relationships, and the legacy they’ll leave. Looking back can include plenty of laughter: Families might retell favorite stories or swap inside jokes. “I have no idea what they’re referencing,” she says, “but it’s almost like they’re recounting the stories.”
Say the four things that matter most
Decades ago, Byock started teaching patients, students, and families that there are four things worth saying to someone before you're forced to say goodbye. Put them in your own words if you like, but here’s how he phrases it: “Please forgive me. I forgive you. Thank you. I love you.”
The first two are there because no relationship is perfect. "Within the history of almost all relationships, there are times of misunderstandings, hurt feelings, anger—sometimes real transgressions," Byock says. You can be specific about what you’re asking forgiveness for, or you can keep it general. “Dad, please forgive me, because I know I haven’t been the perfect son,” Byock offers as an example. “And I forgive you for the times that I felt misunderstood and harshly judged by you.”
In conversations between parents and children, Byock suggests adding an expression of pride. A parent might say, “I’m so proud to be your dad.” “Who else on the planet can tell your child how proud you are to be their mom or their dad?” he says. “That is a gift that keeps on giving.” A son or daughter can reverse it: “I’m so proud to be your daughter.” When the person dying is young, Byock focuses especially on this kind of affirmation.
It’s a good conversation to have even if no one is sick. Byock had it with his own mother in October 2003, prompted by the galleys of his book. They sat together, and he said nearly all of it, including thanking her for being his most steadfast supporter. There were tears, and they talked for an hour. A month later, his mother died suddenly of an undiagnosed heart condition. "I miss her," he says. "But there was nothing critically important left unsaid between my mom and me."
Reassure them about what they're leaving behind
Much of what frightens people at the end isn't about them. It's about everyone else.
Vlahos sees it most clearly with the matriarch of a family—the woman who called all the kids every Sunday, who hosted every holiday. She describes a patient who seemed to be holding on, and whose sons finally said the thing she needed to hear to pass peacefully: “I promise I'm still going to call Dad every Sunday. I promise we're still going to have Christmas.”
Vlahos remembers a patient who was told, “I promise to make sure your grandson knows you.” "I think that matters a lot more than people think," she says.
Then there are the reassurances almost no one thinks to offer. Brazzal

title: Rogue AI agents created fake online identities in another hacking attempt
summary: Yet more rogue AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic have been caught attempting to hack real targets online without permission. The discoveries add to a growing list of previously unknown incidents that have alarmed AI safety experts and intensified pressure for greater oversight of frontier systems. According to a report from the UK's AI Security […]
full_text:
Yet more rogue AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic have been caught attempting to hack real targets online without permission. The discoveries add to a growing list of previously unknown incidents that have alarmed AI safety experts and intensified pressure for greater oversight of frontier systems.
Rogue AI agents created fake online identities in another hacking attempt
AISI said AI agents from OpenAI and Anthropic displayed unprecedented ‘autonomy and deception’ in their test.
According to a report from the UK’s AI Security Institute, which evaluates frontier models from top AI labs before they are released, agents powered by OpenAI’s GPT-5.6-Sol and Anthropic’s Mythos 5 went “engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations.” This included trying to insert malicious code into an open-source project by pressuring real people in charge of it, AISI said. “In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project’s maintainer to approve the code.”
AISI said the attempts, which it detected on July 28th, “were unsuccessful” and had not resulted in real-world harm. However, the organization noted that the incident marked “the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.”
Unlike OpenAI’s rogue agent that attacked Hugging Face, AISI said this was “not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment,” or sandbox. Safeguards usually imposed on the models had been disabled as part of testing, AISI said, and they had also been permitted access to the internet. “To measure what these models can genuinely do, we test them under conditions that reflect what a capable human attacker could do,” AISI said.
The incident stemmed from a single AISI evaluation where agents were tasked with solving a cybersecurity challenge, such as finding a piece of protected data. The challenge was run 122 times across multiple models and all runs were conducted in AISI’s research environment, which uses “virtual machine sandboxing to isolate the agents from other AISI infrastructure.” AISI’s investigation found that in 10 of those, “an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations.” Of 19 such actions, almost all — 17 — came from Anthropic’s Mythos 5.
In its post-mortem of the incident, AISI identified several key factors it said contributed to the unsanctioned agent behaviors. It said the agent was persistent, pursuing avenues like trying to trick real people through “deception that, until recently, had been largely theoretical.” The task was also hard, which the organization said could push agents to be more “creative” in their problem-solving. Compounding matters were deficiencies in how internet use was monitored, with AISI suggesting that more dedicated surveillance could have identified the problem sooner. Finally, the organization said the agent hadn’t been specifically instructed not to leverage its internet access or deploy deceptive social engineering techniques in pursuit of its goal. “Previously, it was not clear that such instructions were necessary when using models with alignment training,” AISI said.
AISI said the incident should be “interpreted with caution and nuance” but warned the agent’s actions “show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours” that “were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.”
In a blog post, OpenAI acknowledged the breach that happened during AISI’s testing and said it is “committed to working across the industry to strengthen shared practices for conducting high-risk evaluations safely.” OpenAI also disclosed another breach, this time from an external cybersecurity testing partner Irregular, where it said models had been mistakenly granted internet access during cybersecurity exercises. OpenAI said Irregular notified it of the breach on July 29th.
“In the coming weeks, we will review our own approach to third-party testing, including how we identify higher-risk evaluations, agree on scope, assess requests to enable internet access or lowered safeguards, set expectations for isolation, credential handling, monitoring, and stop conditions, and establish clearer incident-notification and escalation processes,” OpenAI said.
Anthropic posted a less comprehensive response on X, largely emphasizing that the models’ standard safety features had been disabled and that they had not been given “any specific restrictions on how the internet should be used.” It said it was working closely with AISI to gather more details for its own investigation.
The findings add to an increasingly tangled mess of rogue actions from agents during testing, many of which only come to light after dedicated hunting and which feature models not released to the public. The unwillingness or inability of AI labs to contain their products has sparked concern over how such breaches could go unnoticed, the safety of frontier AI systems, and worries over the general lack of transparency and oversight the industry faces. These latest disclosures will likely intensify pressure on the federal government for a more comprehensive framework governing AI models following what reports suggest is a vague and poorly-defined testing plan from the Trump administration, and could add to growing calls for some form of slowdown or pause on AI development.

title: Sunbird relaunched its iMessage app for Android users after three years away
summary: Sunbird Messaging is back on the Google Play Store, offering Android users blue bubble privileges in iMessage complete with reactions and high quality videos for $2.99 a month. Apple and Google have made cross platform messaging better in recent years with support for RCS, but Android users can still cause issues in iMessage group chats, […]
full_text:
Sunbird Messaging is back on the Google Play Store, offering Android users blue bubble privileges in iMessage complete with reactions and high quality videos for $2.99 a month. Apple and Google have made cross platform messaging better in recent years with support for RCS, but Android users can still cause issues in iMessage group chats, like breaking reactions and replies.
Sunbird relaunched its iMessage app for Android users after three years away
The company claims it has addressed the security flaws that shut down its operation in 2023.
Android Authority reports that after Sunbird shut down nearly three years ago due to security issues, the company says its new setup addresses those, and that “Any message moving through our infrastructure is protected in transit and released once it’s delivered,” while media you send or receive is deleted “typically within 48 hours and never longer than 72.”
Your messages are encrypted on your phone before they leave it, encrypted in transit over certificate-pinned connections, and encrypted at rest on your device, using strong AES-256 encryption. On the final leg to an iPhone, your message is protected by Apple’s iMessage end-to-end encryption, which Sunbird never modifies, intercepts, or weakens.
Sunbird’s CEO Danny Mizrahi told Android Authority that “an independent security auditing firm tested its rebuilt Sunbird app,” and reported “no critical vulnerabilities.” Mizrahi also added that, “When a user connects iMessage, their Apple ID password is used once to set up the session and then destroyed. We do not store the password, and we do not keep an authentication token that would let us sign in as them later.”
You can also access Google Messages and SMS from Sunbird, and support for integrating WhatsApp and Facebook Messenger is coming later this year, along with an AI assistant that can summarize chats and draft replies.

title: Ring upgraded its peephole doorbell camera to 2K
summary: Ring has debuted a new version of its smart doorbell camera that's designed to be easily installed as a replacement for a door's peephole without drilling or running wires. The Peephole Cam 2K is a replacement for the brand's Door View Cam that first debuted in 2019 and, alongside a sleeker design, it features a […]
full_text:
Ring has debuted a new version of its smart doorbell camera that’s designed to be easily installed as a replacement for a door’s peephole without drilling or running wires. The Peephole Cam 2K is a replacement for the brand’s Door View Cam that first debuted in 2019 and, alongside a sleeker design, it features a bump from 1080P to 2K video recording, some tracking upgrades, and a cheaper price. It’s available for preorder now for $99.99 with shipping expected later this month.
Ring upgraded its peephole doorbell camera to 2K
The new Peephole Cam 2K can be installed without having to drill holes or modify a rental property.
As with previous models, the Peephole Cam 2K is divided into two halves that connect to each other through your door’s peephole. On the outside there’s a camera, doorbell, speaker, and microphone, while inside are additional electronics including a removable battery good for an estimated 120 days of use between charges. But there’s no preview screen on the inside, so to check who’s at your door you’ll need to reach for your phone or a compatible smart display.
That inconvenience is potentially outweighed by being able to see and respond to whoever’s at your door from anywhere, even when you’re not at home. The Peephole Cam 2K will also deliver real-time motion alerts with brief descriptions of what its camera is seeing, and you can limit its motion detection to specific regions of its wide-angle 140-degree field-of-view so that passing cars, for example, don’t trigger alerts. However, features like being able to review recorded events for up to 180 days and specific alerts for detected packages are only available with an additional Ring Protect plan.

title: Traveling this summer? Don’t go without these essential gadgets
summary: There's a chance that you've already taken your big summer trip. If not, August and early autumn are wonderful times to travel. No matter when or where you go, there are some products that can make the boring parts of your trip more fun, and the fun parts of your trip even better. We picked […]
full_text:
There’s a chance that you’ve already taken your big summer trip. If not, August and early autumn are wonderful times to travel. No matter when or where you go, there are some products that can make the boring parts of your trip more fun, and the fun parts of your trip even better.
Traveling this summer? Don’t go without these essential gadgets
A couple dozen tech upgrades to make this summer’s trip(s) the best they can be.
If you buy something from a Verge link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
We picked a couple dozen products at a range of price points to best suit your budget. At the affordable end, we found a wearable reading light that’s great for reading on a plane or in a hotel while you’re adjusting to a different time zone. We also included affordable belt bags, sunglasses, item trackers, and other practical products (as well as picks that are just for fun).
Even though we’re recommending these gadgets for your upcoming trip, they’ll likely become staples that you bring on several adventures in the future.
Summer travels often mean enduring scorching temperatures while waiting in long lines or “enjoying” a meal on a patio. I like the refillable water reservoir on Nitecore’s izzCool 10 Pro fan, which it uses to blast you with a fine mist that’s a more effective way to cool down. You can also swap that reservoir for a larger plastic water bottle with enough capacity to use the fan’s misting mode all night long as a makeshift humidifier.
Sitting in front of the TV isn’t exactly the best use of summer travel time, but sometimes it’s solace after a long, tiring day. For Switch 2 owners, the Jsaux OmniCentro dock will let you easily connect your console to any TV that has an HDMI port. It’s no bigger than many phone chargers, yet it can display your games at up to 4K.
The ability to beam video wirelessly from your phone, tablet, or laptop to any modern TV sounds like a far-flung idea of the future. Well, apparently we sort of live in the future now because Belkin’s wireless HDMI display adapter can perform the feat with ease. Once its transmitter and receiver are plugged into your video source (via USB-C) and TV (via HDMI and the TV’s USB-A port), you can view videos at up to 1080p at 60Hz.
While many people may use their Nintendo Switch 2 at home, it really shines when you use it on the go. The console is a fantastic travel companion because its 7.9-inch screen is vivid and great at keeping up with fast-paced games. While it has only been on shelves for just over a year, the Switch 2 library of games is fantastic, and it’s backward-compatible with almost all original Switch games.
SwitchBot Standing Circulator Fan
Hopefully, wherever you’re going has air conditioning or good air circulation to keep you cool while you’re resting. If not, well, one solid option we recommend is the SwitchBot Standing Circulator Fan. The battery-powered option is height-adjustable, comes with a built-in (but optional) nightlight, and best of all, has a sweeping 3D air pattern that is great at circulating air compared to other similarly priced fans.
Ugreen Nexode Pro wall charger
Most of us have gone on at least one trip where the charger we brought didn’t have enough ports to keep everything charged. Ugreen’s Nexode Pro 160W five-port charger is an all-in-one solution if you’re traveling with many gadgets. It has four USB-C ports (two of which can supply up to 140W) and one USB-A port, foldable plugs, and a screen that shows how much power each device is receiving.
It’s not particularly difficult to find luggage that has a suitable number of pockets and good build quality. It’s not even that hard to find those features without spending a ton of money. Something that’s harder to find (and that Timbuk 2’s Copilot Luggage Roller does so well) is silent wheel movement. Whether you’re running through the airport or walking down the street, its skateboard-esque wheels don’t make a peep.
AR glasses are a luxury purchase if you really want to get immersed in your movies, TV shows, and games. Typically, they’re around $500 if you want a pair with good optics and solid build quality, but $299 gets you Xreal’s new A01 Plus, its lightweight USB-C glasses that are surprisingly good. They have fewer features compared to pricier options, but they’re a great first pair if you’re curious about the tech.
Traveling with a gaming handheld isn’t always easy. The likes of Nintendo’s Switch 2 and Valve’s Steam Deck are pretty hefty. If you’re a gamer who’s looking to travel lighter, but doesn’t want to resort to a cheap-looking handheld, Anbernic’s RG Rotate is a slick Android system with a clever rotating screen. The handheld is powerful enough to run modern Android games, along with plenty of retro titles via emulators.
The Wacaco Minipresso GR2 can turn between 8 and 12 ounces of ground coffee into espresso with the help of a hand-powered pump — no batteries or power required, just hot water. The espresso maker itself is just over half a pound, and everything you need to pull a shot fits neatly into the carrying pouch, making it a great choice for waking up properly while camping.
Nothing beats reading by the pool or at the beach, and the Kobo Clara Colour makes it easy to bring an entire library along. The lightweight, waterproof e-reader can hold thousands of books without taking up precious luggage space, while its color E Ink display makes book covers, comics, and magazines come to life.
Whether you’re catching flights or trying to find your car after a long day of sightseeing, the Pebblebee Clip 5 offers peace of mind. Attached to luggage, keys, or even left in the car, it taps into Apple’s Find My or Google’s Find Hub network to help quickly track down valuables. It can also flash its built-in light or ring your phone if it’s gone missing.
Fujifilm Instax Mini 41
There’s something special about having photos you can actually hold before a summer trip is even over. The sleek Fujifilm Instax Mini 41 makes it easy to quickly capture and print memories from vacations, delivering solid photo quality with a built-in selfie mirror that helps you take photos with friends.
Packing light is a lot easier when you don’t need a separate charger for every device. The Anker Nano Travel Adapter (5-in-1, 20W) works in almost every country thanks to four built-in international plug types. It also features two USB-C ports, two USB-A ports, and an AC outlet, making it easy to keep your phone, camera, e-reader, and other travel essentials charged from one small adapter.
Glocusent LED Neck Reading Light
If you don’t want to keep your travel companions awake, Glocusent’s neck reading light offers an easy solution. The wearable light provides adjustable luminance, making it easy to read in a shared hotel room, on an airplane, or anywhere else without relying on bright overhead lights that might disturb the person next to you.
DJI Osmo Mobile 7P
The DJI Osmo Mobile 7P stabilizes your smartphone for smoother videos, making it easy to capture everything from walking tours to kids running on the beach without shaky footage. A built-in tripod and extension rod make hands-free filming easy, while it can automatically track your movements, adjust framing, and even start or stop recording with a simple hand gesture.
Garmin InReach Mini 3
If your plans involve backpacking, camping, or heading anywhere cell service isn’t guaranteed, the Garmin inReach Mini 3 helps you stay connected when your phone can’t. It lets you send and receive text messages, share your location, and trigger an SOS alert in an emergency via satellite, while offering multi-day battery life in a rugged, lightweight package.
Whether you’re sightseeing or relaxing by the beach, the stylish Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses let you capture photos and videos without constantly reaching for your phone. They’re useful in other ways too, with the ability to play music, make calls, livestream your adventures, and use Meta AI to tr

title: Disney says it’s ‘exploring’ adding a free tier to Disney Plus
summary: Disney is looking into launching a free streaming option. When asked about Disney's plans for free, ad-supported streaming during an earnings call on Wednesday, Disney CEO Josh D'Amaro confirmed the company is "exploring a free product for consumers." D'Amaro added that a free tier will help drive growth and expand the streaming service's reach "to […]
full_text:
Disney is looking into launching a free streaming option. When asked about Disney’s plans for free, ad-supported streaming during an earnings call on Wednesday, Disney CEO Josh D’Amaro confirmed the company is “exploring a free product for consumers.”
Disney says it’s ‘exploring’ adding a free tier to Disney Plus
Like other major streamers, Disney Plus is facing increasing competition from free-to-watch services like YouTube.
D’Amaro added that a free tier will help drive growth and expand the streaming service’s reach “to a customer segment that’s more price sensitive.” Though D’Amaro said that there’s “nothing specific to announce today,” he noted that a free tier is “definitely something that we’re considering.”
In July, Business Insider reported that Disney’s chief product and technology officer, Adam Smith, brought up the possibility of a free streaming tier during a company town hall. Streaming services like Disney Plus, Netflix, and HBO Max are facing increasing competition from YouTube, which has taken steps to make its platform look more like TV with “Stations” that play content 24/7 and a way for creators to organize videos into “seasons.”
Next year, Disney plans to expand the Disney Plus ecosystem as part of efforts to make it the “digital centerpiece” of the company. That includes “bringing together games, merchandise, and other experiences, while offering increased personalization, exclusivity, and benefits for subscribers,” according to D’Amaro. The company also announced that it’s partnering with TikTok to bring “Disney-centric fan-created content” to the short-form video feed in Disney Plus.

title: Coldcard exploit could boost demand for regulated bitcoin exposure, analysts say
full_text:
Coldcard exploit could boost demand for regulated bitcoin exposure, analysts say
Cantor sees positive read-through for crypto custody providers, while FRNT says the breach could drive some investors toward bitcoin ETFs.
- Cantor said the Coldcard wallet exploit could provide a positive read-through for crypto-related equities tied to institutional adoption.
- FRNT Financial said the exploit could increase demand for bitcoin ETFs as some investors seek alternatives to self-custody.
- Both firms said the long-term impact is likely to be adaptation rather than abandonment, with cold wallet providers improving security while some investors gravitate toward ETFs.
The Coldcard wallet exploit, which saw investors’ bitcoin 
Investment bank Cantor said the breach may reinforce the appeal of publicly traded crypto firms linked to institutional adoption.
The bank said the exploit could drive Coldcard users toward managed custody providers, potentially benefiting firms including Robinhood Markets (HOOD), Coinbase Global (COIN), BitGo Holdings (BTGO), Bullish (BLSH), eToro Group (ETOR) and Gemini Space Station (GEMI) through increased customer inflows.
“The read-through is second-order but we would expect that token flows to custodians and exchanges will increase following the hack,” Nico Pasquariello, a digital asset specialist, said in the Wednesday note to clients.
The exploit allowed attackers to steal bitcoin from users who had opted for self-custody, underscoring that holding one’s own private keys still requires trust in the hardware and software used to generate and manage them.
The exploit, which researchers say stemmed from a flaw in the wallet's firmware, has resulted in at least 1,816 bitcoin, worth about $114 million, being drained from more than 5,200 addresses since July 30, underscoring the risks even self-custodied assets face when wallet security is compromised.
FRNT Financial echoed that view, saying the exploit exposed a key tradeoff in self-custody. While many bitcoin holders prefer to control their own assets, they still place their trust in the hardware and software used to generate private keys.
"The reaction within the BTC community to the exploit was one of heartbreak," FRNT wrote in a Wednesday report, noting many affected users had followed long-standing best practices around self-custody.
The firm compared the incident to the 2023 "Milk Sad" exploit, in which flawed key generation led to the theft of roughly $900,000 in digital assets. Rather than undermining self-custody altogether, FRNT said it expects the latest breach to spur wallet providers to strengthen their products as users demand greater security assurances.
For investors unwilling to accept the operational risks of managing private keys, the growing availability of spot bitcoin ETFs provides an increasingly attractive alternative, FRNT said.

title: Crypto-backed Michigan House incumbent loses primary despite $2M PAC support
summary: A Midwest Democratic primary that raised accusations of payback from the cryptocurrency industry ended with the unseating of two-term incumbent Shri Thanedar.
full_text:
Crypto-backed Michigan House incumbent loses primary despite $2M PAC support
A Midwest Democratic primary that raised accusations of payback from the cryptocurrency industry ended with the unseating of two-term incumbent Shri Thanedar.
Michigan State Representative Donavan McKinney won a Democratic primary against incumbent House Representative Shri Thanedar in a race that raised accusations of payback by the cryptocurrency industry.
McKinney won the primary for Michigan’s 13th Congressional District with 51.9% of the vote against Thanedar’s 48.1% as of Wednesday, the New York Times reported. The primary saw a cryptocurrency-backed political action committee (PAC) spending more than $2 million on media in an attempt to re-elect Thanedar, who has voted in favor of many bills favoring the industry while in Congress.
Election results for Democratic primary in Michigan’s 13th congressional district. Source: The New York Times
McKinney, considered by many to be a progressive challenger to two-term Thanedar, has already received support from the Democratic National Committee and the Democratic Socialists of America on his primary victory. During the campaign, he accused the crypto industry of “paying my opponent back for helping Trump make over $1 billion since taking office,” likely referring to Thanedar’s voting record.
Protect Progress, the super PAC responsible for funding the ads supporting Thanedar and opposing McKinney, is affiliated with Fairshake, a group backed primarily by crypto companies Coinbase and Ripple. After spending more than $170 million in the 2024 US election cycle on similar races involving pro- and anti-crypto candidates, Fairshake and its affiliates have poured additional millions of dollars into media for politicians in this year’s primaries in several US states ahead of the November general election.
Related: Nigel Farage to resign from UK Parliament amid crypto “gift” scandal, will stand in by-election
In addition to voting for bills like the GENIUS Act and CLARITY Act in the House of Representatives, Thanedar also reportedly lost more than $600,000 in the second quarter of 2026 after investing $3.7 million of campaign funds into crypto companies.
”Washington has spent too long serving billionaires and corporate interests,” said McKinney in a Wednesday X post. ”I will always only serve the people I represent.”
McKinney will face off against Republican candidate Taras Nykoriak in the November election. Cointelegraph sought a comment from McKinney’s campaign on Wednesday but did not receive an immediate response.
PAC-supported candidate wins Washington primary
In addition to Protect Progress’ efforts in Michigan, the Fairshake affiliate Defend American Jobs spent more than $65,000 on media to support Republican Amanda McKinney (no relation to the Michigan candidate) in Washington’s 4th congressional district. McKinney will face off against Democrat John Duresky in November, with both candidates securing more than 30% of the vote in Tuesday’s primary to advance to the general election.

Western Union brings stablecoin remittances to Visa network with Stablecard
The remittance giant is rolling out Stablecard across 37 markets, targeting cross-border payments and consumers seeking US dollar-denominated savings in volatile economies.
Western Union has partnered with stablecoin infrastructure provider Rain to launch Stablecard, a digital wallet and Visa-branded card that enables users to hold and spend a US dollar-backed stablecoin, marking one of the company’s biggest moves into blockchain-based payments.
On Wednesday, Western Union said Stablecard allows users to hold, receive, transfer and spend USDPT, a US dollar-backed stablecoin issued by Anchorage Digital Bank on the Solana blockchain.
Stablecard launched in 37 markets, with Western Union aiming to expand availability to more than 60 markets by the end of the year. Users can receive Western Union money transfers directly into a USDPT wallet, transfer funds to compatible crypto wallets and exchanges and spend their balances anywhere Visa is accepted, including through Apple Pay and Google Pay.
The launch reflects Western Union’s effort to expand its role in the global remittance market as stablecoins gain traction for cross-border payments. The product is aimed at remittance recipients and consumers in countries with volatile local currencies, offering them the ability to hold savings in a dollar-backed digital asset while spending through existing payment networks.
Western Union unveiled USDPT in May as part of its broader digital asset strategy, describing it as a stablecoin designed to align with the framework established under the GENIUS Act, the recently enacted US law that sets federal rules for the issuance and oversight of payment stablecoins. The company has already expanded the token’s ecosystem through exchange partnerships, with Bybit adding support for USDPT trading and transfers in June.
Related: Mastercard expands support to USDC, PYUSD, RLUSD stablecoin settlement
Stablecoins push deeper into global money transfers
Stablecoins are increasingly reshaping cross-border payments as users seek faster and lower-cost alternatives to traditional remittance services, particularly in Africa and South America.
The trend has prompted established money transfer companies to expand into digital assets. Western Union rival MoneyGram recently launched MGUSD, a US dollar-pegged stablecoin on the Stellar network. The token is designed to integrate with the MoneyGram app through a self-custodial wallet, allowing users to hold dollar-denominated balances, send funds globally and convert them into local currencies when needed.
However, stablecoins are not a universal solution for remittances. A recent Bank of Italy study found that stablecoin-based remittances did not consistently outperform traditional payment channels on cost or speed. The researchers attributed much of the remaining friction to fiat currency on- and off-ramps, where converting between bank deposits, cash and digital assets accounted for most transaction costs and settlement delays.
