title: Olympic champion curler Muirhead comes out of retirement
summary: Winter Olympic gold medallist Eve Muirhead revokes her retirement, saying being Team GB's chef de mission at this year's Games has inspired her to return to curling after four years away.
full_text:
Olympic champion curler Muirhead revokes retirement
- Published
Winter Olympic gold medallist Eve Muirhead has reversed her retirement, saying being Team GB's chef de mission at this year's Games has inspired her to return to curling after four years away.
The 36-year-old will team up with two-time Olympic silver medallist Bobby Lammie in mixed doubles this season - the pair having won the world title in 2022 - with a view to ultimately reaching the Alpes 2030 Games.
Four-time Olympian Muirhead stepped away from competing after winning gold in Beijing four years ago, and subsequently spoke about the mental health challenges she experienced towards the end of a 15-year struggle to win gold.
The Scot was Team GB's chef de mission at the Milan-Cortina Games in February and says that "brought back emotions that I had not felt for a long time".
Muirhead explained that being away from curling gave her the chance to try new things, take on new physical challenges, and enjoy the sport "without the pressure I had placed on myself for so many years".
- Olympic champion Muirhead retires from curling 
  - Published11 August 2022
- How Team GB is leading the way in curling's arms race 
  - Published11 February
- How does curling work? 
  - Published4 February
"But the competitive side of me never disappeared," she added. "The more time I spent around elite sport and curling, the more I began to wonder whether I still had something to give on the ice.
"I know how demanding the road to an Olympics is, but I am returning from a very different place. I feel refreshed, physically strong and excited by the challenge. I would not be coming back unless I believed I could perform at that level again."
Muirhead's gold medal-winning team-mate Vicky Drummond is also returning to the sport to rival her - and a third member of that rink, Jen Dodds - in the GB Curling mixed doubles programme.
Drummond, 32, says being part of the BBC Sport team in Cortina in February rekindled her passion for competing, and that she wants to show her young daughter Sophie that "becoming a mum doesn't mean your ambitions have to end".
"More than anything, I want my return to mean something beyond the ice," said the intensive care nurse, who will partner Euan Kyle.
"I want Sophie to grow up knowing that it's never too late to chase something that excites you. If she grows up believing that anything is possible because she watched me try, then this journey will already have been worth it.
"I have no idea where this road will lead, but I'm excited to find out."
Analysis: Friends become rivals in fascinating twist
Spending time with Muirhead and Drummond in Cortina earlier this year, it was clear how much both revelled being back in the elite sport environment and how much curling meant to them.
In Muirhead's case, there was always going to be a void after the all-consuming job of chef de mission ended abruptedly when the Games did.
And her near-zealous completion of Hyrox events around the world - and at a predictably elite level - spoke to the competitive fire still inside her.
At 36, she is still young and will return revived - and with the cachet of having not just won Olympic gold - but dealt with the stresses and strains of that journey. And she will do so with arguably the best sweeper in the sport alongside her.
Drummond is even younger and returns with a different motivation. That is not to say she'll not be just as competitive as her close friend.
The battle between them, and Dodds, to be part of GB's pre-eminent pairing as we move towards the next Winter Olympics will be fascinating.

title: Mourinho, Ferguson & search for new club - what next for Smalling?
summary: Snubbing university, genetics testing for supplements, Sir Alex Ferguson and Jose Mourinho - Chris Smalling is not your ordinary footballer.
full_text:
Mourinho, Ferguson & search for new club - what next for Smalling?
- Published
It is clear from the first answer of a fascinating 45-minute chat that Chris Smalling is no ordinary footballer.
A career that took the 36-year-old from non-league Maidstone to a Champions League final in the space of three years, has, so far, led to 580 club appearances in three countries, playing the majority for Sir Alex Ferguson or Jose Mourinho, plus 31 England caps and trophies with Manchester United and Roma.
It has now brought Smalling and his family back to the north west of England to figure out his next steps.
Smalling has plans for his career after playing but presently, he is focused on finding a new club.
"I know my body now better than when I was 26 and that's shown in the games I'm playing," he said.
"When I was younger, I remember Sir Alex was implementing certain things, like Ryan Giggs doing yoga.
"When you get beyond 30, each year is precious in terms of enjoying playing and being passionate about football.
"Actual training is a very short time. The longevity and recovery starts very early in terms of what I'm eating and doing between sessions, even down to my supplements now.
"In pre-season we have blood tests and the clubs make recommendations. I went one step further and kind of had genetics testing, which goes deep into everything. A lot of my supplements were changed because of that."
Smalling was an ever-present for Al-Fayha in the Saudi Pro-League last season, something he is particularly proud of.
His career is not over. Yet wind back 18 years and Smalling did not imagine he was destined to come anywhere near as far as he has.
"It wasn't even plan D," he recalled.
"I was playing at Maidstone, but I was going to university to study financial economics.
"I had everything set out. I already had my A levels, and I was looking at other non-league clubs near Leicester because I still wanted to play.
"It was very late in the summer when the opportunity came around. I knew it was a slim chance even to be offered but I needed to do everything I could."
The offer was from Fulham. Roy Hodgson watched one practice game, called Smalling into his office and offered a contract.
"It wasn't even a full week," said Smalling. "I didn't have any time to get my head around it. I was just in total shock."
It wouldn't be the last time Hodgson put Smalling into a position where he had no time to think.
He was part of the Fulham squad that travelled to Blackburn for a Premier League game on 17 January, 2010. As it turned out, the then 20-year-old would play no part in the 2-0 defeat.
For him, the important part of the trip took place the previous evening.
"There had been a lot of talk about other clubs but not Manchester United," he said.
"Roy pulled me off the coach, said Fulham had accepted a bid and Sir Alex was coming to the hotel in 45 minutes. I called my mum first but then I was sitting in the room thinking it was going to be a bit awkward and what questions could I can ask him?
"Literally, we were there for about at least a couple of hours. He was so calming and reassuring.
"Even I was doubting it because they had all these great centre-backs. I wanted to develop and wondered 'how do I fit in?'.
"He told me I would get a chance and he believed in me.
"To be able to share the dressing room and the pitch and have conversations with him, is just incredible."
It is that personal side which Smalling feels sets the great managers apart.
To outsiders, his relationship with Mourinho is characterised by a public criticism from the Portuguese in November 2016 around an unwillingness to play through an injury.
That is not how Smalling views it.
"For United or Roma, Jose picked me for most games because we had a good relationship and he trusted me.
"It's very easy to influence younger players but the beauty of Sir Alex and Jose is that they were able to create that belief in senior players. A lot of managers can give good team talks but if you look at some eye-to-eye, see the passion and real belief that 'it's going to happen' senior players follow and the rest lock in. That's the beauty of top-class manager.
"In that situation, I was having injections in broken toe because he had created that mentality in me that I could do anything, even if, maybe, I shouldn't. I had reached the limit of the amount [of injections] I could have, had to stop in a warm-up and he was disappointed.
"It gave me even more belief because it was easy to choose another centre-back but he wanted me."
More than a player
Smalling remains in contact with Mourinho and wished him good luck when he took over at Real Madrid this summer.
He has no plans to follow his old boss into coaching.
"I don't think it will be my route," he said. "I'm quite comfortable with the next stage.
"I'm working on an education programme for young players partnering with the Global Institute of Sport that's going to be coming out shortly. I've got three or four of these types of projects.
"Once my football career comes to an end, I can put more time to them but at the minute it's all focused on playing because I have that passion and drive and physically my stats are good."
Whoever signs Smalling will get more than just a player.
He had a positive input in Al-Fayha's off-field development, ensuring the gym was suitable for the standards an elite modern-day player demands.
He is proud that at all his previous clubs he is remembered fondly and made a positive impact on and off the pitch.
Turning down that university offer was a good move.
"It would have been the safer route," he said.
"In that first year, I was not earning a lot of money. I was playing for the reserves and the 19th man for the first team, travelling around but not quite on the bench. There was no guarantee I was going to earn more money.
"When I signed for United, it was a four-year contract. At the end of the first year, I signed a new one, another a year later and another 18 months after that.
"There was always this carrot. I never took anything for granted."

title: Iran anthem protest: Female footballers ‘proud’ to become Australian
summary: Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh refused to sing Iran anthem at Asian Cup, now granted Australia citizenship.
full_text:
Iran anthem protest: Female footballers ‘proud’ to become Australian
Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh, who refused to sing Iran anthem at AFC Cup, now granted Australian citizenship.
Two former Iranian female footballers say they are “proud” to have been granted Australian citizenship after being branded traitors at home for refusing to sing the national anthem before a game.
Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh, who were granted Australian citizenship at a ceremony on Wednesday overseen by Minister for Home Affairs Tony Burke, were members of a group of seven from Iran’s delegation who asked for protection from the host country following the high-profile protest during the Women’s Asian Cup in March.

With their demands for protection an embarrassment for Iran’s leaders but lauded by United States President Donald Trump, five of them later changed their minds and returned home.
“Yesterday was a truly special and unforgettable day for me. I feel proud and deeply grateful to become an Australian citizen,” Ramezanisadeh said in a statement.
“After everything we’ve been through and all the challenges we faced, this moment means more than words can express,” Pasandideh said.
A week after seeking asylum, the pair were pictured smiling and training with Australian club Brisbane Roar, which on Wednesday congratulated them.
“What they have been through since February is more than most people deal with in a lifetime,” a spokesperson for the club said.
“To see them arrive at this point is something everyone here at Brisbane Roar is glad to have had a small part in,” they added.
“Queensland is their home now. If they ever want to pull on a training top and come back out with us, the door will always stay open.”
The plight of the rest of the team remains unclear since their return to Iran.
Reporters of the AFP news agency saw them cross into their homeland from Turkiye on a bus wearing the national team tracksuits and with their hair covered.
Soon after, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on X that the players and their support team were “children of the homeland and the people of Iran embrace them”.
By returning, they had “disappointed the enemies [of Iran] and did not surrender to deception and intimidation by anti-Iran elements”, he added.

title: Russian strikes kill six in Ukraine as Moscow intercepts hundreds of drones
summary: Ukraine officials say three people killed in Kharkiv region and three in Sumy, as Russia says it intercepted 605 drones.
full_text:
Russian strikes kill six in Ukraine as Moscow intercepts hundreds of drones
Ukrainian officials say three people killed in Kharkiv region and three in Sumy region, as Russia says it intercepted 605 drones.
Russian strikes on eastern Ukraine have killed at least six people overnight, local authorities have said, as Moscow shot down 605 Ukrainian drones over its territory and the annexed Crimean Peninsula.
Rescuers worked on Thursday to douse fires and clear debris in Balakliya, in the eastern Kharkiv region, after Russian strikes on homes killed three people, authorities said on the Telegram messaging app. Vitalii Karabanov, head of the military administration in the front-line city, said the victims were two women and a man.

- list 2 of 3Nine killed in escalating long-range strikes between Russia and Ukraine
- list 3 of 3Russian missile attack kills 14, injures 27 in Ukraine’s Kyiv region
Three more people were killed overnight and at least 19 others wounded in Russian attacks in the northern region of Sumy. Twelve people were wounded in the city of Sumy following an attack with guided aerial bombs, according to Ukrainian police.
Separately, two people were wounded in a Russian attack in the Dnipropetrovsk region, according to Oleksandr Ganzha, the head of the regional military administration.
A drone attack on a van wounded six people in the southern region of Kherson, the regional administration said on Telegram.
In Ukraine’s Black Sea area, a Russian attack damaged a foreign-flagged ship loaded with wheat, killing a crew member and causing a fire, Oleh Kiper, Odesa regional governor, said.
Ukraine’s seaport administration said the vessel Mera Queen, under the flag of Guinea-Bissau, was hit late on Wednesday.
For more than a month, Russia has been ramping up its efforts to strangle Ukraine’s trade and export routes, launching near-daily attacks on the country’s Black Sea ports.
Meanwhile, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces had shot down Ukrainian drones overnight. “During the night … air defence systems intercepted and destroyed 605 Ukrainian aerial drones,” the ministry said in a statement.
Local authorities reported that a logistics centre belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries had been “slightly damaged”. The incident comes days after another Wildberries warehouse was struck by drones in the Tver region, northwest of Moscow.
At least 20 warehouses owned by the company have been attacked since July 18. Kyiv alleges that the online retailer, Russia’s largest, plays a crucial role in Moscow’s war effort by supplying dual-use items that can be used for military purposes.
Later on Thursday, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed the military hit two oil refineries deep inside Russia, the Bashneft-Novoil refinery in the republic of Bashkortostan and the Slavnet-Yanos refinery in the Yaroslavl region. There was no immediate comment from Russian authorities on the claim.

Ex-Bangladesh cricket captain Shakib’s home petrol-bombed in Hasina fallout
Former Bangladesh captain Shakib Al Hasan’s home attacked after joining former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s event.
Windows were smashed and petrol bombs hurled at former Bangladesh cricket captain Shakib Al Hasan’s residence after he joined ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s first public media interaction since her 2024 removal from power, in which she pledged to return in December.
Police said a group of people attacked Shakib’s ancestral home in Magura town, about 170km (105 miles) southwest of the capital Dhaka, on Wednesday, causing a fire on the upper floor of the residence. The property was unoccupied at the time, and no injuries were reported.

The Reuters news agency was unable to reach Shakib for comment on the attack. The attack came hours after Shakib, a former Awami League lawmaker, joined a virtual event organised by the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia in New Delhi.
During the audio address, Hasina reiterated that she would return to Bangladesh, where she has been sentenced to death.
Shakib, who was elected to parliament as an Awami League candidate in January 2024, has remained outside Bangladesh since the student-led uprising that toppled Hasina’s government. He faces multiple investigations, including over allegations of murder, embezzlement, fraud and money laundering.
“I will return to my people,” Hasina said. “I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, but still I have to go back.”
The event, held on the second anniversary of her ouster, was Hasina’s first public interaction with the media since she fled Bangladesh in 2024. Hasina also said the ban on the Awami League, the party she led for more than four decades, should be lifted after it was barred from political activity following her ouster.
Bangladesh’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned Hasina’s media appearance, describing it as “an affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh” and warning that allowing her to address the media from India could harm bilateral relations. Hasina, 78, has been living in New Delhi since August 2024. Bangladesh has sought her extradition from India, which says the request is being examined under its legal procedures.
In November 2025, Bangladesh’s war crimes tribunal sentenced Hasina to death in absentia over the deadly crackdown on the 2024 student-led uprising, charges she has dismissed as politically motivated.

title: Messi scores his first goals since World Cup as Inter Miami beat San Luis
summary: Lionel Messi scores his first goals since Argentina's World Cup final defeat to Spain, as Miami win 4-2 in Leagues Cup.
full_text:
Messi scores his first goals since World Cup as Inter Miami beat San Luis
Lionel Messi scores his first goals since Argentina’s World Cup final defeat by Spain, as Miami win 4-2 in Leagues Cup.
Lionel Messi scored his first two goals since the World Cup and took the career scoring lead in the Leagues Cup as Inter Miami overcame an early deficit to beat Atletico de San Luis 4-2.
The match at Nu Stadium on a rainy Wednesday night was delayed 30 minutes in the second half due to lightning in the area.

Messi scored in the 11th and the 44th minutes. He has 14 goals in 12 Leagues Cup matches – one ahead of Los Angeles FC’s Denis Bouanga for most in the tournament’s four-year history.
Telasco Segovia and defender Micael also scored, and Noah Allen had three assists as Inter Miami extended its unbeaten streak to eight matches.
Messi returned to Miami’s starting lineup in his second match since the World Cup, where he led Argentina to their second straight final appearance before La Albiceleste lost 1-0 to Spain.
The 39-year-old played 37 minutes as a substitute in a 2-2 draw with the Columbus Crew on Saturday.
After being held off the scoresheet against Columbus, it didn’t take Messi long to make an impact on Wednesday. He fired a long cross from Allen past Andres Sanchez to equalise after David Rodriguez put San Luis ahead with a header four minutes into the match.
Messi finished from close range later in the first half and assisted on Micael’s header in stoppage time.
Rafa Llorente also scored for San Luis.
Messi led Miami to the Leagues Cup title in 2023 shortly after his arrival to the club. Inter Miami reached the final again last year, losing 3-0 to Seattle in a match that ended with a brawl involving Luis Suarez.
The veteran forward appeared to spit towards a member of the Sounders’ staff and grabbed at least one Seattle player by the neck during the melee, resulting in a six-match tournament suspension.
That means Suarez, who has seven goals in the past four matches, was not available on Wednesday and will not play in this year’s tournament.

title: Pakistan beat West Indies to end 8 away Test losing streak and draw series
summary: Pakistan win first away Test in three years, beating West Indies by eight wickets in Trinidad to draw two Test series.
full_text:
Pakistan beat West Indies to end 8 away Test losing streak and draw series
Pakistan win first away Test in three years, beating West Indies by eight wickets in Trinidad to draw two Test series.
Pakistan ended its eight-match losing streak away from home in cricket Tests with a resounding eight-wicket victory against the West Indies to level the series.
First innings century-maker Abdullah Shafique and Babar Azam, in his first series since being reappointed as captain, led Pakistan to 77-2 with unbeaten knocks of 24 runs each as the visitors achieved victory shortly after lunch on Day Four of the second Test on Wednesday.

Babar knocked off the target by hitting back-to-back sixes against left-arm spinner Jomel Warrican, whose six-wicket haul in the first innings had limited Pakistan’s lead to 43 runs.
West Indies won the first Test by 90 runs at Tarouba. In the second Test, spinners Sajid Khan and Ali Usman utilized favourable conditions on a wearing wicket of Queen’s Park Oval to ensure Pakistan remained unbeaten in a Test series against the West Indies since 2000.
Pakistan lost the wickets of Imam-ul-Haq, brilliantly snapped up by Justin Greaves in the slips cordon for 9 in Jayden Seales’ first over Wednesday, and Azan Awais was bowled by Shamar Joseph for 18 before Shafique and Babar sealed the win inside four days.
Earlier, West Indies had set up a modest target of 75 runs after it got bowled out for 117 with off-break bowler Sajid (4-32) and left-arm spinner Usman (4-39) sharing eight wickets between them.
Opening batter Brandon King could not bat in West Indies’ second innings due to a back injury sustained on Day Three when he ran out Babar with a spectacular direct throw from short cover.
Resuming on 106-3 – only 60 runs ahead – the resistance of West Indies’ tailenders ended quickly, with Usman picking up the wickets of Kemar Roach and Joseph.
Greaves, the last recognised batter, played on to seamer Mohammad Ali’s delivery back onto his stumps after adding just two runs to his total as he attempted a cross-batted shot, but got a big inside edge.
Pakistan’s last Test win away from home came against Sri Lanka in 2023 during Babar’s first tenure as captain, before Shan Masood led the side for nearly three years during which Pakistan lost 3-0 in Australia; 2-0 in South Africa; and 2-0 in Bangladesh.
Masood was eventually relieved of the captaincy after Pakistan’s dismal run in red-ball cricket, but the return of Babar as skipper saw Pakistan lose the first test at Tarouba last week, in Pakistan’s eighth loss away from home in three years.

title: Senate committee set to vote on whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress
summary: Republicans on the Senate Homeland Security Committee want to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress after he refused to answer their questions about the government's response to the COVID-19 pandemic.
full_text:
Senate committee set to vote on whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress
Anthony Fauci, the 85-year-old retired health official who helped lead the U.S. government's response to the coronavirus pandemic, faces a contempt-of-Congress vote Thursday.
The punitive measure under consideration by the Republican-led Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee comes after he refused to answer lawmakers' questions in a hearing last week, citing his Fifth Amendment right to avoid self-incrimination.
In an opening statement, Fauci said that the committee chairman, Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., has "an unhinged obsession" with him and suggested the hearing was convened in an attempt to trick Fauci into lying under oath.
"Therefore, although it pains me to do so because of the respect I have for the legislative branch of government and my decades-long record of cooperating with Congress," Fauci said, "under the advice of my attorneys, I will invoke my right under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution to refrain from answering your questions."
Fauci told the committee he had answered many of their questions already during previous testimony.
Fauci, the United States' leading infectious disease expert during the pandemic, has long sparred with Paul over the origins of the pandemic. In the days leading up to last week's hearing, Paul released more than 1,000 pages of Fauci's private diary entries, pointing to them as evidence that he masked private uncertainty about what caused the pandemic.
During that hearing, Paul indicated that Fauci shouldn't be concerned about testifying, given his immunity from prosecution over pandemic-era conduct. That immunity stems from a pardon that Fauci received from President Joe Biden for conduct between 2014 and January 2025 — a pardon that the then-president described as "preemptive" given Republican scrutiny of Fauci.
The 2025 pardon wouldn't protect Fauci from any prosecution stemming from conduct after that date, including any remarks made during present-day congressional testimony.
If Republicans do vote to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress, the Justice Department will then decide whether to pursue a criminal prosecution. While prosecutions are rare, two former Trump advisers — Steve Bannon and Peter Navarro — were imprisoned on contempt-of-Congress charges during the Biden administration.
Many Democrats now see a similar risk for Fauci, pointing to the prosecution of other former government officials whom President Trump is critical of, including his former FBI director, James Comey.

full_text:
As their warships encircle Japan, what signals are China and Russia sending?
The pair aim to show they aren’t boxed in by the first island chain and that Moscow can project power despite the Ukraine war
The recent joint patrol between China and Russia around the Japanese archipelago showed how the nations’ military cooperation was becoming “progressively more ambitious”, analysts said.
The Japanese defence ministry revealed on Tuesday that three Chinese naval vessels – Type 055 and Type 052D missile destroyers alongside a Type 903 support ship – were spotted moving southwest through the Korea Strait between Sunday and Monday.
The ministry said that Maritime Self-Defence Force vessels and patrol aircraft conducted surveillance and intelligence-gathering operations along the route taken by the Chinese naval ships.
The manoeuvre followed the recent conclusion of a 17-day China-Russia joint patrol.
According to a map posted to social media by the Japanese defence ministry, the Chinese and Russian naval vessels transited through the Miyako Strait near Okinawa on July 16. They then sailed near the Ogasawara Islands and through the waters south and east of Japan before finally reaching the La Perouse Strait between Hokkaido and Russia’s Sakhalin Island on July 27.
This means that, including their passage through the Korea Strait, the Chinese warships conducted a full circuit around Japan.

title: Starbucks Korea raided by police after ‘Tank Day’ campaign sparks public outrage
summary:
Coffee chain has faced backlash over marketing promotion tied to anniversary of Gwangju massacre

South Korean police have raided the headquarters of Starbucks Korea as part of an investigation into a marketing campaign accused of trivialising the country’s 1980s pro-democracy movement.

Investigators searched the building in southern Seoul on Tuesday, police said on Wednesday. No further details were released, although South Korean media reported that officers also searched the homes of the Starbucks Korea executives.

Continue reading...
full_text:
South Korean police have raided the headquarters of Starbucks Korea as part of an investigation into a marketing campaign accused of trivialising the country’s 1980s pro-democracy movement.
Investigators searched the building in southern Seoul on Tuesday, police said on Wednesday. No further details were released, although South Korean media reported that officers also searched the homes of the Starbucks Korea executives.
The coffee chain triggered a public outcry after launching a range of stainless-steel reusable tumblers it called “SS Tank” and declaring 18 May “Tank Day”. The date marks the anniversary of the 1980 Gwangju uprising, when pro-democracy demonstrators were brutally suppressed by South Korea’s then military-backed government.
The campaign also used the slogan “Thwack it on the table!”, which many interpreted as a reference to a notorious 1987 police claim that the student activist Park Jong-chul died after investigators “hit the desk with a thwack”. Authorities had falsely used the phrase to conceal the fact that Park had died by torture during an interrogation.
The backlash over the coffee chain’s marketing campaign prompted Shinsegae Group, which owns a 67.5% stake in Starbucks Korea, to cancel the promotion within hours and dismiss the company’s chief executive. The Shinsegae chair, Chung Yong-jin, later issued a televised apology.
Starbucks Korea closed all of its stores nationwide on 22 June for mandatory training in history and social awareness.
The police investigation was launched after complaints from relatives of victims of the Gwangju crackdown, in which, official records say, about 200 people were killed.
South Korea’s transition to democracy gained momentum in 1987, when the authoritarian president Chun Doo-hwan, whose government had overseen the Gwangju crackdown, accepted constitutional reforms introducing direct presidential elections after months of nationwide pro-democracy protests.

title: ‘Performative reductions’: Labor MPs and business groups urge Burke against sweeping immigration changes
summary:
MPs say they are anxious for the government to avoid cuts to family and humanitarian visa categories

Major business groups have urged Labor to suspend its immigration changes and consult further with industry about how to get more skilled workers into the country, amid questions about looming Labor tweaks on permanent migration.

With home affairs minister Tony Burke delaying an anticipated immigration speech by at least one week, some Labor MPs say they are anxious to avoid major changes to the family and humanitarian visa categories, with one urging against “performative reductions” in migration in response to One Nation.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Major business groups have urged Labor to suspend its immigration changes and consult further with industry about how to get more skilled workers into the country, amid questions about looming Labor tweaks on permanent migration.
With home affairs minister Tony Burke delaying an anticipated immigration speech by at least one week, some Labor MPs say they are anxious to avoid major changes to the family and humanitarian visa categories, with one urging against “performative reductions” in migration in response to One Nation.
But other Labor sources characterised Burke’s as tweaks to existing settings, with an expected focus on enforcement of existing rules and small pruning of various programs.
“Tony’s doing an absolutely fantastic job of ensuring, that our immigration program which is so vital for us economically, vital for our vibrancy … the world’s most successful multicultural nation. But it must be properly calibrated,” said energy minister Chris Bowen.
Burke was to deliver a National Press Club address on Thursday about migration policy, but withdrew on Tuesday with a spokesperson telling media “some elements of the speech would not be finalised” in time.
The ABC reported measures could include tougher family visa rules, capping backpacker numbers, or restrictions on asylum seekers. Burke’s office would not confirm media reports, and senior sources in the government remained tight-lipped on the changes.
Some sources said they believed media and stakeholder focus on Burke’s speech had been overegged, characterising the changes as more “surgical” adjustments across multiple migration areas, and downplaying major changes to work, family or humanitarian visas.
Another Labor source said they expected Burke’s speech would focus on how Labor plans to cut permanent migration to 185,000 per year – a target the government has cited in budget papers – rather than any cuts below that number.
That figure includes about 132,000 skilled migration places and 52,000 partner and family visas.
But potential cuts to either stream are already facing pushback from business groups and government members.
Outside what will be detailed in Burke’s speech, his department recently announced that skilled migrants who are already in Australia would be given priority for permanent residency, which could help lower total migrant numbers, but also decrease the pipeline of available workers.
The Minerals Council of Australia called on the government to “suspend skilled migration changes and consult industry” more closely on those changes.
MCA’s CEO Tania Constable said the reforms would “make it harder for mining and other sectors”, raising fears about skills shortages and risks to project timelines, earnings and the economy. She said mining companies were already struggling to find workers.
“Demand from these sectors for specialised skills is already growing faster than migration pathways can adapt, and industry is frustrated and impeded by slow updates, credential barriers and settlement constraints,” Constable said.
Acting prime minister Richard Marles denied rumours of a disagreement with Burke in a cabinet meeting on Monday.
“Migration obviously plays a really significant part in our economy, but it needs to happen at a sustainable rate,” he said.
Pauline Hanson told News 24 that she didn’t care if employers groups thought a migrant crackdown “is going to affect their businesses.”
“I don’t care. My concern is for those Australians that can’t get a roof over their head,” she said.
Labor MP Jerome Laxale told the ABC that Labor would strive to meet its 185,000 permanent migration target.
“If that requires tweaks to our policy to do so, we just have to do that,” he said.
Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry CEO Andrew McKellar said it would be a “concern” if Labor was to trim working holidaymakers, while cutting family visas would also be a disincentive to attracting skilled workers.
“The government should proceed with caution, we don’t want to shoot ourselves in the foot,” he said.
“It would have a damaging impact if the government was to try to curtail those categories in a draconian way.”
Master Builders Australia CEO Denita Wawn added the datacentres boom would need a new boost to construction workers, calling for tradespeople to be prioritised.
“Migrant tradies ultimately contribute to far more homes than they consume, especially when they reside here over the long term,” Wawn said.
Guardian Australia also spoke to several Labor MPs who said the government should tread carefully around partner visas, warning any cut to family categories would raise anxiety across communities.
One MP said everyone including the government should stop being “hysterical” about migration numbers, and wanted to see firmer pushback by Labor against One Nation’s immigration rhetoric.
“I am against performative reductions, I am in favour of steady migration … Getting skilled people in from overseas is imperative,” they said.
“[Burke is] possibly driven by desire to be seen to be reducing migration rather than anything of substance.”
Another MP said they would be concerned if the government reduced Australia’s humanitarian intake, while a third said cutting backpackers could be a way forward.
One MP said there was confusion among those outside the cabinet who had not yet been advised of any changes. All said the issue was complex, and while reform across the system was needed, that the messaging critical – especially amid the rise of Hanson and One Nation’s anti-immigration agenda raising fears in migrant communities.

title: Labor faces fierce backlash from gambling giants as Coalition and Greens push for new controls on inducements
summary:
Despite reports the PM wants Labor’s bill to be passed in full or withdrawn, Anika Wells insists she is prepared to negotiate

Labor will face strong opposition from gambling giants if it accedes to Coalition and Greens demands for a tough new ban on financial inducements for betting, part of closely watched Senate dealmaking expected within days.

Despite reports on Thursday that the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, could insist Labor’s bill to limit advertising for online sports betting be passed in full or be withdrawn, the communications minister, Anika Wells, insisted she was prepared to negotiate.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Labor will face strong opposition from gambling giants if it accedes to Coalition and Greens demands for a tough new ban on financial inducements for betting, part of closely watched Senate dealmaking expected within days.
Despite reports on Thursday that the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, could insist Labor’s bill to limit advertising for online sports betting be passed in full or be withdrawn, the communications minister, Anika Wells, insisted she was prepared to negotiate.
After a two-day inquiry including sensational evidence that gambling companies allegedly provided illegal drugs and access to sex workers to keep problem gamblers betting, Wells is waiting on amendments from the Coalition, due to be finalised in party room meetings next week.
“We’re having constructive discussions,” Wells said on Thursday. “I’ll continue to do that with my counterparts. We’d love to see this pass.
“I would wait for the Coalition to form a position and to put those amendments to the government, exactly as this process always plays out when we try to put any piece of legislation through the Parliament.”
Debate on the bill was supercharged by sensational evidence from former NRL player Luke Bateman and veteran anti-gambling campaigner Tim Costello this week.
They alleged problem gamblers had been supplied with cocaine, alcohol and sex workers, part of efforts from gambling company VIP managers to keep big-spending punters betting as long as possible.
Betting giants who appeared before the inquiry at a later session said there was no evidence to support the allegations.
Opponents of Labor’s bill have pointed to a landmark inquiry report delivered by the late MP Peta Murphy in June 2023.
Murphy’s committee recommended the government “prohibit all online gambling inducements and inducement advertising, and that it do so without delay”.
Separately last month, Labor’s national conference agreed to explore how to better prevent online gaming and social media platforms from offering “embedded inducements” within video games and social media accounts designed to incentivise and normalise gambling among children and young people.
The Labor backbencher Jerome Laxale on Thursday challenged the opposition to bring forward constructive amendments to advance a ban on the financial incentives offered to punters.
He said he would welcome Labor’s draft laws “being strengthened in the Senate”.
The acting opposition leader, Jane Hume, said the shadow communications minister, Sarah Henderson, was negotiating for new controls over inducements, suggesting gambling companies were using them to “essentially entice people to maintain their problem gambling addiction”.
“We want to make sure that these laws are actually delivering on their purpose, that they find the balance between what is a legal pastime, but making sure that we protect the most vulnerable,” she said.
The chief executive of lobby group Responsible Wagering Australia, Kai Cantwell, said further bans on inducements were a non-starter for the gambling industry, drawing a distinction between inducements and “promotions”.
He accused members of the Senate committee considering Labor’s bill of mistakenly grouping together appropriate promotions and illegal inducements.
“They are about product differentiation and customer loyalty,” he told ABC radio.
“We provide personalised services to the entire customer base. That is the benefit of account-based gambling. We understand our customers’ betting trends and patterns and can provide tailored consumer protections to our customer base as well, based on trends of betting and potential risk factors.”
Labor MPs including Louise Miller-Frost and Alicia Payne told Guardian Australia this week that the draft legislation should be significantly strengthened.

title: Alan Jones’s alleged victim denies ‘fabricating’ claims against broadcaster during robust cross-examination
summary:
Former 2UE and 2GB radio broadcaster is facing 22 charges. Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty

  • Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A former student sports star has denied in a Sydney court that he “fabricated” indecent assault allegations against broadcaster Alan Jones after he lost his police job and fell on “extremely hard times”.

Jones’s defence barrister, Gabrielle Bashir SC, on Wednesday suggested to complainant J during cross-examination that he had a financial motive to report his alleged indecent assaults 20 years after the incidents.

Continue reading...
full_text:
A former student sports star has denied in a Sydney court that he “fabricated” indecent assault allegations against broadcaster Alan Jones after he lost his police job and fell on “extremely hard times”.
Jones’s defence barrister, Gabrielle Bashir SC, on Wednesday suggested to complainant J during cross-examination that he had a financial motive to report his alleged indecent assaults 20 years after the incidents.
The former police officer, now in his 40s, had earlier told Sydney’s Downing Centre local court that Jones had touched him sexually when he was a teenager. J was being financially supported by the broadcaster at the time.
J told the court earlier this week that Jones gifted him a Nokia mobile phone, a Nissan car and a stipend which rose from $350 to $600 a week over a nine-year period.
“Your evidence in relation to payments into your account from Belford [company] and the increase in payments has been you trying to assert Jones had an ulterior motive for making payments to you?” Bashir asked the former athlete.
J replied: “No, I wasn’t trying to assert that.”
Bashir continued: “Do you accept that those payments were for the purpose of assisting you for your training and competition and living expenses?”
“Yes,” complainant J told the court.
The cross-examination of J could not immediately be reported as it was subject to an interim non-publication order. But judge Glenn Walsh lifted the order on Thursday afternoon.
Jones is facing 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges in relation to six men. He has pleaded not guilty.
The court heard on Wednesday that J resigned from the police after he was convicted of assault and found to have breached the force’s code of conduct.
Bashir put to him that he lost his income of $120,000 a year and had to pay child support and rent, and had to move in with a relative. J denied during cross-examination that he had a gambling problem.
Challenged by the judge about the relevance of J’s financial problems to his complaint about the alleged indecent assaults by Jones, Bashir said: “A complaint like this, if successful, is a stepping stone to civil proceedings. I will be putting that to him.
“It is an opportunity to then go on to make a claim and an opportunity to cast himself in a different light after he lost his job,” Jones’s barrister told the court.
J earlier this week told the court he had decided to go to NSW police about his alleged assaults after seeing in the media that Jones had been arrested and charged in November 2024.
Bashir said on Wednesday during cross-examination: “You had from that moment decided to fabricate that Mr Jones sexually touched you as a young teen?”
“When you sent the email [to police] in November 2024, you did so as part of a decision to fabricate claims Jones sexually touched you as a teen?” Bashir asked.
“No, I wasn’t planning to fabricate anything,” complainant J replied.
Bashir said J hadn’t raised the alleged incidents when he was charged with drink-driving in the mid-2000s, or when he was charged with assault in the early 2020s or when he was subsequently facing termination from the police force.
J agreed he did not raise the allegations at those times.
Asked whether he saw Jones’s arrest as a “life-changing opportunity”, J said he was not after financial compensation and only wanted justice.
“I’ve been clear on this,” he told the court. “I don’t want anything from this. I won’t accept [money]. I don’t want anything but proper justice in relation to this matter.”
Bashir alleged that J gave the police false statements about when Jones had given him the phone and car. The court heard that J originally told police Jones gave him the phone when he was 14 or 15, but he was in fact 18.
J agreed after being shown documents that Jones gave him the car when he turned 18 and had left school, and not when he turned 17, as he had previously told the court.
“At the time I provided the details, I thought that was accurate,” J said on Wednesday.
Bashir suggested J’s claim that Jones increased his weekly stipend after Jones said he had “been a good boy” was also a fabrication. She said his stipend was increased by Jones when he had success in his sport.
Bashir: “Do you accept those payments, to your knowledge, were for the purpose of assisting you with training, competition and living expenses?”
“Yes. He did pay me to assist with training and competing … I don’t know if that was the reason for the increase in the payments,” J told the court.
Bashir then said: “It’s the case, isn’t it, that you are recasting these payments as something sinister when in fact your understanding at the time was that they were anything but?”
“No,” J replied in court on Wednesday.
Bashir’s Thursday cross-examination focused on inconsistencies between his police statement and evidence he gave this week in court.
Bashir pointed out during her cross-examination on Thursday that J had described it as “peck” in his police statement but described it as a “chomping motion” kiss in his evidence to the court.
J conceded that he “might” have got it “wrong” that Jones kissed him with a “chomping” motion during one of the alleged indecent assaults in Canberra.
“I might have got the kiss wrong, but there was definitely a kiss in that room,” he told the court. “I won’t steer away from the fact there was kiss because there was.”
Jones has denied all wrongdoing and said the allegations were either baseless or distorted the truth.
Bashir on Monday argued that the alleged victims in the case were egged on to complain by media rivals, and their reliability and credibility were questionable.
The trial continues.

title: ‘Orange elephant in the room’: Pauline Hanson’s political rise is inspiring racism, inquiry hears
summary:
Former AFL inclusion manager tells inquiry One Nation leader’s conduct is encouraging people to use ‘similar behaviour and words’

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The rise of One Nation is fuelling racism, a federal parliamentary inquiry into racism, hate and violence directed at First Nations people has been told, with high‑profile Indigenous journalists warning the inquiry that 1970s‑style racism “is back”.

The inquiry is holding public hearings in Melbourne this week, hearing evidence from prominent personalities and sporting groups about their experiences of racism, discrimination, violence and harm across Australia.

Continue reading...
full_text:
The rise of One Nation is fuelling racism, a federal parliamentary inquiry into racism, hate and violence directed at First Nations people has been told, with high‑profile Indigenous journalists warning the inquiry that 1970s‑style racism “is back”.
The inquiry is holding public hearings in Melbourne this week, hearing evidence from prominent personalities and sporting groups about their experiences of racism, discrimination, violence and harm across Australia.
Independent Victorian senator Lidia Thorpe asked Tanya Hosch, former inclusion and social policy manager at the AFL and senior consultation with Kind Enterprises, if Hanson’s “rise was increasing racism”, referring to the One Nation leader as the “orange elephant in the room”.
Hosch told the committee that while she had not personally met the politician, she believed the rise of One Nation and the controversial senator “expressed racism” through her public speech and rhetoric.
“I believe many of the things that she says have racist intent and express racism. I do believe that it does encourage people to use similar behaviour and words and actions and I think that is pretty well documented.”
National Indigenous Television’s national Indigenous editor and host of current affairs program The Point, John-Paul Janke, told the inquiry that racism, online hate and discrimination had flourished after the failed voice to parliament referendum in 2023.
Janke said that while he had seen improvements over his nearly 40-year professional career, he had also noticed a steep escalation in online abuse and violence targeting Indigenous peoples.
“I have witnessed an alarming escalation of online racial slurs, of delegitimising First Nations history and expertise, coordinated online pile ons, and sustained abuse aimed at First Nations voices.”
Janke, a Wuthathi and Meriam man from the Torres Strait Islands, said in his work speaking with Indigenous people from remote, regional and metropolitan areas – all had witnessed a rise in racism and hate.
“Online racism is now becoming in-person violence. They are worried that it is escalating. Janke said. “I am a father of four boys, and the racism that I grew up with in the 1970s is back.”
“The names that I was called in the 1970s in far-north Queensland, sadly, [are] being used against my children today. When will it stop?”
Janke, along with Channel 10 journalist and presenter Narelda Jacobs and former Channel 9 morning presenter Brooke Boney, also gave detailed evidence to the inquiry.
They spoke about the increasingly virulent rise of racism, online hatred and the challenges of reporting on First Nations issues in the Australian mainstream media landscape, including recommending cultural awareness training in newsrooms and ensuring and advocating for respectful coverage.
Jacobs, a Noongar woman from Western Australia said that conservative media can also fuel negative perceptions of First Nations people with very little regulation within the sector to address concerns.
“There is very little accountability when it comes to media outlets sprouting hate and racism, there are no consequences if you do lodge a complaint,” Jacobs told the inquiry.
“It’s seen by those media organisations as engagement that fuels their purpose; they continue publishing articles or opinion pieces, because it sells.”

Vladimir Tkachuk, the founder of the private drone manufacturer Uraldronzavod, was rushed to intensive care on Wednesday after a bomb planted beneath his Mercedes exploded, according to Russian state media, citing emergency services. His bodyguard was killed in the explosion.

Images circulating on social media showed the charred wreckage of a Mercedes, with blood stains visible on the pavement nearby.
Uraldronzavod is one of several private drone manufacturers that sprang up in Russia after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. full_text:
Tehran would control Hormuz strait's inbound traffic in deal, according to reports
Welcome to our live coverage of the latest in the ongoing Middle East crisis.
Iran said a deal with Oman to reopen the strait of Hormuz is close to being finalised, with reports suggesting Tehran would have control over ships entering the Gulf through the strategic waterway.
Both countries, which sit on opposite ends of the narrow strait, have been engaged in talks to jointly manage the key shipping route, which has been effectively closed since the start of the war in February. Iran has insisted the strait would not operate as it did before the conflict, as an open international waterway that carried about a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supply, as it seeks greater control over the flow of maritime traffic through the channel. Several media reports, citing sources familiar with the talks, suggest Oman would oversee outbound shipping through the strait.
But despite reports of potentially one of the biggest concessions yet to Iran, Reuters news agency said Iranian sources rejected US President Donald Trump’s claims that a deal to reopen the strait was imminent, saying important details were still to be agreed.
“The concession has already been made regarding some form of control over Hormuz,” one of the sources said.
Iran has also said that reopening the strait would hinge on the US lifting its blockade of Iranian ports.
Trump told Fox News earlier this week that talks over the strait were “moving along nicely”, adding that the strait “is going to be open very soon”.

In Yemen, meanwhile, the Iran-backed Houthis said yesterday they had attacked two Saudi oil tankers with ballistic missiles, amid the group’s maritime blockade of the kingdom.
In other developments
Two Israeli reserve soldiers were killed and four seriously injured in an explosion southern Lebanon, the military said this morning – the first Israeli deaths since the fragile truce between Israel and the Iran-backed militant Hezbollah in June. An Israeli military official told the Associated Press that “an explosion was detonated” when the soldiers entered a site in the village of Majdal Zoun and that the nature of the explosive was under review.
One person was killed and 12 wounded in an Israeli strike in the southern Lebanese town of Tebnine, Lebanon’s health ministry said. The Israeli military earlier told residents of the southern Lebanese village of Mansouri to evacuate – the first such order in more than a month – saying it was in response to a Hezbollah ceasefire violation.
The escalations came despite ongoing US-backed talks in Rome aimed at ending hostilities. Israel requested that yesterday’s talks with Lebanon end three hours early, a source told AFP, saying the Israeli delegation’s head had blamed alleged “misleading leaks” by the Lebanese side. But the talks are expected to resume today for a third and final day.
A Houthi military spokesperson said its latest attacks targeted the eighth and ninth Saudi oil tankers since the start of its blockade last month. Saudi authorities had no immediate comment.
Shipping traffic through the Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb straits – the key maritime chokepoints in the Gulf – reduced significantly yesterday from the previous day, shipping data showed.

title: Israeli strike that killed journalist in Lebanon was war crime, say rights groups
summary:
Investigation by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty and Legal Agenda shows Israel deliberately attacked Amal Khalil and colleague Zeinab Faraj knowing they were civilians

An Israeli strike that killed Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil and injured her colleague Zeinab Faraj in April was a war crime, three rights organisations said on Thursday.

Investigations from Human Rights Watch (HRW), Amnesty International and Legal Agenda showed that Israel deliberately and directly attacked Khalil and Faraj, with apparent knowledge that they were civilians. The organisations called for the attacks to be investigated as war crimes, while HRW called for states to halt arm sales to Israel and put targeted sanctions on Israeli officials responsible for ongoing crimes.

Continue reading...
full_text:
An Israeli strike that killed Lebanese journalist Amal Khalil and injured her colleague Zeinab Faraj in April was a war crime, three rights organisations said on Thursday.
Investigations from Human Rights Watch (HRW), Amnesty International and Legal Agenda showed that Israel deliberately and directly attacked Khalil and Faraj, with apparent knowledge that they were civilians. The organisations called for the attacks to be investigated as war crimes, while HRW called for states to halt arm sales to Israel and put targeted sanctions on Israeli officials responsible for ongoing crimes.
Deliberate attacks on civilians, which both journalists were, is a war crime. Israel has killed at least 15 journalists in Lebanon and 210 in Gaza since 2023, according to the UN human rights office.
The reports also indicated that Israel delayed Lebanese ambulances from reaching Khalil and Faraj for hours – at one pointing dropping stun grenades on Lebanese Red Cross workers and firing on their ambulances.
The delay in rescue might have led to Khalil’s death, as hospital reports indicate that she might have still been alive hours after an Israeli strike toppled a building on top of her and Faraj.
“The evidence is clear that the Israeli military knew, or should have, that Faraj and Khalil were civilians, but attacked them anyway, and then prevented paramedics from rescuing them for hours,” said Ramzi Kaiss, Lebanon researcher at Human Rights Watch.
Israel said it “regrets any harm caused to journalists,” and that the journalists were killed “as part of a series of events” during which two Hezbollah military operatives were killed. There was about two hours between the initial strike that killed the two men Israel said were in Hezbollah, and a second strike that targeted a building the journalists were sheltering in.
Amal Khalil was a 42-year-old journalist working for al-Akhbar, a Lebanese newspaper, while Zeinab Faraj was a 21-year-old freelance camerawoman and photojournalist. Both had been active in covering the war in Lebanon over the last three years.
On 22 April 2026, the pair drove to the village of al-Tiri, south Lebanon, to verify reports that Israeli troops had left the area. They drove behind a car carrying Ali Nabil Bazzi, a municipal official of the city of Bint Jbeil, as well as Mohammed Hourani, a friend of the mayor.
Al-Tiri was in what Israel calls its “security zone” in southern Lebanon, which its troops occupy. Amnesty said that despite the Israeli military calling it a military zone and barring people from going there, it is still required to distinguish between civilians and combatants.
At 2.25pm, after entering al-Tiri, the car carrying Bazzi and Hournai was struck, killing the men. Khalil called the Lebanese civil defence and requested assistance.
The civil defence drove to the entry of the village, where they were told to stop at a military checkpoint while they waited for authorisation from the Israeli military to enter the village safely.
Rescue crews operating in areas of south Lebanon where fighting is taking place or which the Israeli military occupies must coordinate with the “mechanism”, a deconfliction channel, to get safe passage. Among others, the Israeli military must give approval for requests for civil defence to get safe passage.
By 5pm, the UN peacekeeping force in Lebanon had given a safe route for civil defence to follow to enter the town, but Israel had not yet given its approval.
While waiting for the civil defence to arrive, Faraj and Khalil left their car and sought shelter elsewhere. Israeli quadcopters circled low overhead while the two journalists waited, Faraj said.
“The drones came extremely close through the roof, less than a metre from my face and Amal’s,” she said.
At 3.31pm, a member of the Lebanese civil defence called Khalil and urged her to get into her car and drive out of the village, as he had not yet received permission from the mechanism to enter the village. Around nine minutes later, Israel struck the journalists’ car, injuring both women.
“Glass and debris flew towards us. My ear felt like it burst. She [Amal Khalil] was bleeding heavily from the nose and head and had shrapnel wounds in her arm and thigh; she couldn’t move her leg,” Farj said.
The two women crawled into a nearby building for shelter. They both continued calling people, asking for assistance, but were told they could not be rescued until authorisation was given from the mechanism.
At 4.25pm, Israel conducted a third strike, bombing the building where they were sheltering, collapsing it and burying both women under the rubble.
At 5pm, permission was given to the Lebanese Red Cross to enter the village. They were able to evacuate Faraj, who had a fractured skull, severe injuries to her right leg and eye, and a crushed hand. Rescuers could not rescue Khalil, who was trapped under rubble.
The rescuers came under attack by an Israeli quadcopter, which dropped a stun grenade near them. Witnesses also said they heard bursts of gunfire during the evacuations, and HRW reviewed photographs of bulletholes in the ambulances consistent with small arms fire.
The rescuers were forced to withdraw with only Faraj.
The Israeli military finally granted the request for rescue crews to re-enter the town at 8.15pm. Khalil’s body was recovered at 11pm. 
 An examination of her body at the nearby Tebnine hospital showed that she probably died at 7pm – two-and-a-half hours after she was struck for the last time. She was trapped under the rubble during that time, waiting to be rescued, while the Israeli military prevented rescue crews from saving her life.
All three organisations have demanded accountability for Khalil’s killing, and described it as part of a larger pattern of impunity by the Israeli military towards civilians.
“The impunity enjoyed by Israeli forces for the killing of journalists and other civilians in Lebanon over the past three years has enabled the Israeli military to continue with its unlawful airstrikes, including direct attacks on civilians,” said Heba Morayef, director for the Middle East and north Africa at Amnesty International.
“It is well past time that the international community impose a comprehensive arms embargo on Israel,” Morayef added.

title: Trump Labels Abdul El-Sayed a Hateful ‘Communist’
summary: The President attacked the Democratic U.S. Senate nominee from Michigan.
full_text:
President Donald Trump didn’t take long to attack Abdul El-Sayed, the winner of Michigan’s Democratic primary for the U.S. Senate race, as “a man of hate” who was “full of sh-t.”
During a campaign-like event in Las Vegas on Wednesday afternoon, Trump accused the 41-year-old progressive Democrat seeking to become the first Muslim U.S. Senator of being a “communist” who “hates” Israel and Jewish people.
“This guy hates Jews. Somebody said, ‘Oh that’s a little strong.’ No, he hates Jews and he hates Israel,” Trump said.
Trump continued: “He’s a man of hate, and now he’s going around saying, ‘No, I love everybody.’ He doesn’t love everybody. Put him in office, you’re going to find out what he loves.”
El-Sayed previously told TIME that he does not consider himself a socialist or communist, saying, “I actually think that at the small and local scale, capitalism is a great way to allocate resources, as long as everybody has access to it.” He has also rejected accusations of antisemitism, repeating on Wednesday, “My commitment to Jewish safety is the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters.”
Trump had earlier claimed on social media that El-Sayed’s primary victory was “great news” for the Republican Party, while he also without evidence suggested that there were voter irregularities in Michigan and that the general election could be “rigged.”
Speaking to CNN Wednesday evening, El-Sayed clarified that he was “opposed to unconditional military aid for any country,” including Israel, and that taxpayer dollars should instead go to services like healthcare, schools, and roads.
As for Trump’s attacks, El-Sayed joked that he’s “glad” Trump at one point called him a “lovely gentleman;” El-Sayed added: “a lot of people think so.” But El-Sayed also called on Trump to refocus his priorities.
“We’re living through an affordability crisis that is generational, people are paying nearly $5 in gas because of a war he started, and half the time, if he’s not talking about me, he’s talking about the drapes in his ballroom,” El-Sayed said. “So at the end of the day, I invite the President to focus on what I’m saying.”

title: Why Sandisk and Western Digital crashed 10% and what it means for bitcoin
full_text:
Why Sandisk and Western Digital crashed 10% and what it means for bitcoin
Strong earnings from SanDisk and Western Digital were not enough to satisfy investors, raising questions about whether capital is beginning to rotate from AI winners into crypto.
- Sandisk and Western Digital fell roughly 10% in pre-market trading as their forward outlooks failed to match elevated expectations.
- Sandisk and Western Digital have gained more than 3,000% and 550%, respectively, over the past 12 months, propelled by the AI boom and leaving assets such as crypto and precious metals in the rearview mirror.
- Now with AI momentum cooling, gold surging and bitcoin holding above $64,000, crypto may be preparing for a resurgence.
Sandisk (SNDK) and Western Digital (WDC), two of the biggest beneficiaries of the AI storage boom, were both 10% lower in pre-market trading Thursday, despite reporting strong quarterly results.
Sandisk posted record fourth-quarter revenue of $8.97 billion and non-GAAP EPS of $39.25, comfortably beating expectations. Western Digital also delivered a double beat, reporting revenue of $3.75 billion, up 44% year over year, while its gross margin surged to 54.4%. Despite those results, both stocks are now trading roughly 50% below their all-time highs.
The problem was guidance. Sandisk’s first-quarter outlook came in below expectations, with projected revenue of $10.7 billion versus the $11.2 billion analysts had estimated. Its EPS guidance also fell short. Western Digital’s first-quarter outlook was solid, but after a 500% run, investors were looking for another blowout beat.
Sandisk and Western Digital have gained more than 3,000% and 550%, respectively, over the past 12 months, propelled by the AI boom and leaving assets such as crypto and precious metals in the rearview mirror.
In addition, Sandisk’s board of directors has also approved an additional $14 billion share buyback program, bringing the total authorization to $15.5 billion.
But with the AI trade beginning to stall, a rotation may be taking shape. Gold has risen more than 7% over the past few days, while bitcoin is holding above $64,000 and shrugging off the Coldcard exploit with little reaction.
Crypto traders may view these indicators as a signal of a change in momentum, given the prevalent narrative that investors have been rotating capital into AI with bitcoin one of the major casualties.

The investment brings the company’s total raised to $106 million across seven funding rounds since November 2021.
- JPYC Inc. raised 6 billion yen ($38 million) in an extension of its Series B funding round to accelerate the expansion of its yen-pegged stablecoin.
- New investors in the latest round include AZ-COM Maruwa Holdings, a major Japanese logistics company.

JPYC Inc. raised 6 billion yen ($38 million) in an extension of its Series B funding round to accelerate the expansion of its yen-pegged stablecoin.
The investment brings the company’s total raised to $106 million across seven funding rounds since November 2021, according to venture capital data site Tracxn.
New investors in the latest round include AZ-COM Maruwa Holdings (9090), a major Japanese logistics company.
AZ-COM plans to settle payments in JPYC with its clients, including Amazon Japan. Its network of around 2,300 partners is made up of subcontractors, drivers and so on. The move marked the first large-scale corporate use of a stablecoin for daily business operations in Japan.
JPYC is one of the most prominent stablecoins pegged to the Japanese yen with a market cap of $55.5 million, according to data tracked by CoinGecko.
Stablecoins are digital tokens pegged to the value of a traditional financial asset, usually a fiat currency. The market is overwhelmingly dominated by tokens pegged to the U.S. dollar. The yen stablecoin sector is growing, helped by adoption among some of Japan’s largest financial institutions, but remains negligible in the context of the USD-dominated market.

The two largest cryptocurrencies are the only CoinDesk 20 members in positive territory as altcoins fall out of favor.
- Bitcoin is outperforming the broader crypto market as traders rotate toward large-cap tokens like bitcoin and ether while altcoins see falling open interest and weak momentum.
- Derivatives data show a cautiously bullish tilt for bitcoin, with rising futures open interest, steady implied volatility and growing upside options bets, while XRP and SOL face leverage-driven pressure.

Bitcoin 
Crypto appears to be moving to the perceived safety of the biggest tokens, with bitcoin and ether 
Altcoin open interest has fallen about 15% over the past month while bitcoin has gained roughly 8%, Ebtikar said. CoinMarketCap’s Altcoin Season index fell one point from Wednesday to 42/100.
“Because Bitcoin has moved into capital markets plumbing with ETFs, basis trading, institutional hedging, and collateral, that flow doesn't need a rally to justify itself. However, most of the altcoin market hasn't made that transition yet,” Ebtikar said.
The divergence, according to Ebtikar, results from projects failing to clearly define how value accrues, making them unable to justify investors’ exposure to their tokens during market declines.
Adding to that, tech stocks are seeing weakness. Nasdaq 100 index fell while the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average rose. That’s after Elon Musk’s SpaceX (SPCX) reported its first results since going public in June.
The IPO unveiled a massive surge in AI-linked capital spending that investors punished, bringing shares down 13% before the closing bell. The AI trade has been widely blamed for capital rotating out of the crypto sector. Its reversal could help renew enthusiasm.
Derivatives Positioning
- Starting with the good news: The long-short taker volume ratio for the crypto futures market flipped bullish for the first time in at least a week, with longs accounting for nearly 52%. Takers are traders who suck liquidity out of the order book by transacting at available prices.
- BTC open interest ticks up, but sustainability remains the question: BTC's futures open interest (OI) increased to 770K BTC. We've been here before several times since early June, but each time the spike was brief, with OI falling back to 740K BTC or lower the following day. What's needed is a sustained rise to show that confidence is being restored and investors are once again willing to on leverage. Other key metrics, such as annualized perp funding rates and 24-hour OI-adjusted cumulative volume delta (CVD), are positive for BTC, supporting a bullish outlook.
- XRP's rising OI alongside falling price: XRP's OI has increased by 5% over the past 24 hours to 2.23 billion tokens while the token's price has dropped to $1.04, the lowest since early July. The combination of a falling price and rising OI is said to confirm, or validate, market weakness. This logic seems reasonable given that XRP's perp funding rates are negative, and its OI-adjusted CVD is among the most negative of the majors, second only to XLM. Some traders, it seems, are preparing for a deeper spot price slide.
- ETH stays lackluster, SOL leverage unwinds: Ether's OI tally remains lackluster, staying below the 14 million ETH mark and showing neither improvement nor position downsizing. That’s in contrast to SOL futures, where OI fell for another day to 60.81 million tokens, having peaked above 76.5 million tokens on June 24.
- Stock-tied perps rank among the most traded contracts: Some of the most traded perpetual futures contracts of the past 24 hours are those tied to stocks, such as SNK, SPCX and SKYHYNIX. These rank up there with crypto market leaders BTC and ETH, indicating persistent demand for trading legacy assets with a crypto flavor.
- Majors show mixed sentiment on 24-hour CVD: Major cryptocurrencies are displaying mixed sentiment, with BTC and ETH leading the pack on positive 24-hour CVD, while SUI, XLM, DOGE, AVAX and XRP sit on the other side. Positive CVD indicates that bulls are being more aggressive, trading at market orders rather than passive limit orders; negative CVD suggests the opposite.
- Implied volatility holds steady for BTC and ETH: Bitcoin implied volatility is unchanged from Wednesday, with the BVIV index continuing to hover near 36%, a level from which it has historically risen toward its mean. The same holds true for the ether index, EVIV.
- Options flow shows growing activity in upside bets: In Deribit options, bitcoin’s 24-hour volume ranking shows increased interest in calls, or bullish bets, at strikes well above the current spot price, such as the $96,000 and $80,000 calls. For ether, the $2,000 call is the most traded of the past 24 hours.
Token Talk
- NEAR traded at $1.68 on Thursday, down 1.8% over 24 hours after slipping from an intraday high of $1.73. The token carries a $2.19 billion market cap, and its price hasn't tracked the ecosystem's AI-compute push higher.
- NEAR's move into AI-compute staking has a demand question looming. The network recently started a staking product that lets holders lock up NEAR to provision the computing power AI applications run on, tying the token's use to compute power rather than governance or speculation. The model only works if the demand behind it is real, said Leo Fan, CEO of Cysic.
- Credits aren't the same as usage. Stake-to-compute setups can give a token a clearer economic purpose, Fan said, but early activity is often driven by incentives, with developers showing up for rewards rather than because they need the compute. The test is whether that usage survives once the incentives normalize.
- Watch three things, Fan said. Utilization, meaning how much of the staked compute is actually being used, workload volume and whether developers keep paying after the subsidies taper. Sustained demand from AI builders will prove the model out. A drop-off when rewards fade would mark it as temporary.
- The read applies beyond NEAR. Tying a token to compute is one of the cleaner attempts to move crypto past governance-and-speculation utility, but it lives or dies on whether the compute gets used. NEAR is the test case others in the AI-crypto space will be watching.

title: NFT startup founder charged with misusing funds from $10 million fundraising
full_text:
NFT startup founder charged with misusing funds from $10 million fundraising
Federal prosecutors say Taj Tarsha misled backers and used investor funds for personal expenses.
- U.S. prosecutors charged Few and Far founder Taj Tarsha with securities and wire fraud tied to a $10 million fundraising.
- The authorities say investor funds meant to build an NFT marketplace were diverted to gambling, crypto trades and personal expenses.
- An internal audit uncovered the alleged misconduct in June 2023. The FAR token debuted in May 2024 but soon became effectively worthless and stopped trading, prosecutors said.
Federal prosecutors in Manhattan charged the founder of non-fungible token (NFT) startup Few and Far with securities fraud and wire fraud.
The prosecutors alleged that Taj Tarsha diverted more than $10 million raised from investors into online gambling, cryptocurrency speculation and personal expenses instead of building the company's marketplace.
The 34-year-old raised the funds from at least 67 investors beginning in February 2022 through Simple Agreements for Future Tokens (SAFTs), the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York said in a statement.
SAFTs give a project’s financial backers the right to receive tokens once they are available. Few and Far’s investors had the right to receive 95 million FAR tokens while funding development of the company’s planned decentralized NFT marketplace.
The prosecutors allege Tarsha began misappropriating investor funds almost immediately after the fundraising closed.
The alleged misconduct was uncovered in a June 2023 audit, according to the statement. Prosecutors claim Tarsha falsely told investors that bonuses he received were tied to token presale milestones and that company funds were being used to advance the project.
Instead, the indictment alleges, he had dismissed most employees while directing one contractor to create the appearance that the marketplace appeared functional.
The government also alleged Tarsha spent investor funds on a loan for a Miami condominium, interior design services and expenses tied to his DJ hobby.
Few and Far launched the FAR token in May 2024, but prosecutors said it quickly became effectively worthless and soon stopped trading.
Tarsha, of Miami, was arrested on June 6, and the case has been assigned to U.S. District Judge Lewis A. Kaplan. Each charge carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison if convicted.
CoinDesk tried to contact Tarsha by email outside of U.S. working hours, and had not received a response by publication time.
