title: Will Pakistan-Saudi-Turkiye alliance actually create a new regional order?
summary: The Mecca Joint Defence Pact brings together countries that sit between Iran and Israel, but will it be effective?
full_text:
Will Pakistan-Saudi-Turkiye alliance actually create a new regional order?
The Mecca Joint Defence Pact brings together countries that sit between Iran and Israel, but will it be an effective deterrent to regional threats?
It was a historic announcement. On Friday, Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a mutual defence pact, building on a similar agreement between Riyadh and Islamabad last year.
But the Mecca Joint Defence Pact, as the agreement is known, has raised questions about the shifting power dynamics in the Middle East region.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3War on Iran: Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan sign defence pact
- list 2 of 3Two civilians killed in Houthi strike on Marib, says Yemen’s government
- list 3 of 3Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan sign joint defence agreement: What’s in it?
Experts have speculated that the deal may mark the beginning of a wider regional alliance that sits between Israel and Iran, wary of both.
While the signatories seek to project a message of strength and unity in the face of regional threats, they have also been cautious about framing the pact as a deterrent.
Analysts note that the three countries have been cautious not to antagonise regional adversaries. It remains unclear the extent to which the pact would force its members to defend their alliance partners.
“We haven’t seen the Mecca declaration yet. We believe it says an attack on one should be considered an attack on all — and ‘should be’ is the operative phrase because that does not mean ‘necessarily’,” Harlan Ullman, the chairman of the Killowen Group advisory firm, told Al Jazeera.
The threats are not distant. Pakistan has been engaged in a border conflict with Afghanistan since February, and it exchanged fire for several days with fellow nuclear power India in May 2025.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, has repeatedly come under attack from Iran and its allies since the outbreak of the United States-Israeli war against Iran in late February.
And Turkiye has fought Kurdish armed groups both inside and outside of the country for years. Tensions with Israel have also increased.
Experts like Ullman say it is as yet unclear how the Mecca Joint Defence Pact might pull its three signatories into any of those conflicts.
“Supposing the Houthis in Yemen attack Saudi Arabia, does that bring in Turkiye? Does that bring in Pakistan? That remains to be seen,” Ullman said.
Shifting regional dynamics
The Middle East has experienced significant upheaval in recent years, most notably since the Hamas attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, and the subsequent Israeli genocide in Gaza.
Decades of threats between Iran and Israel have also culminated in a regional war that has yet to end.
Countries across the Middle East and further afield are now trying to figure out how to deal with the chaos and prepare for the next phase.
Many of the states appear to be putting past differences behind them and deciding that pragmatism is the best path forward in the face of mutual threats.
Turkiye and Saudi Arabia are good examples. The 2018 murder of Saudi journalist Jamal Khashoggi in his country’s Istanbul consulate led to a deep rift between the two countries that lasted for years.
But by 2022, Riyadh and Ankara were seen to put aside their past differences, with the former pursuing a region-wide deescalation strategy, and the latter looking to strengthen its economy.
In the time since, Israel and Iran have exerted pressure on the Middle East, pursuing different visions for the region.
That pressure, however, is understood to have helped to push countries like Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye together.
Establishing deterrence
The Mecca Joint Defence Pact aims to serve as deterrence to any threat the three countries may face.
As Al Jazeera correspondent Osamah Bin Javaid pointed out, each side brings a different strength to the table.
“Each of these countries brings unique capabilities: Pakistan’s battle-hardened military, its munitions and nuclear arsenal, the only one in a Muslim-majority nation,” Bin Javaid said.
“Turkiye, a vital NATO member, brings world-class drone technology and sophisticated defence manufacturing. And Saudi Arabia provides the financial muscle to back it all up.”
The need for new military alliances — and new forms of deterrence against threats — has been amplified amid questions about the US and its reliability. Saudi Arabia, and Turkiye to a lesser extent, have long considered the US a key security partner.
But as foreign policy in the US grows increasingly erratic under President Donald Trump, countries across the world are calling for alternatives.
Experts also point out that Israel appears to be the US’s top foreign-policy priority in the Middle East, leading to concerns about its willingness to defend other allies.
“The Trump administration has said that allies have got to fend for themselves,” Ullman said. “ It’s clear to me that our allies are looking elsewhere.”
While Israel and Iran have shown themselves to be regional threats, the signatories to the Mecca Joint Defence Pact have been careful not to frame the alliance as aimed at any external force.
But experts say the dangers posed by Israel and Iran are clear.
“For all three states, Israel remains the biggest threat to regional security and stability,” Bin Javaid said.
“Iran closely follows within that threat matrix, especially for Saudi Arabia after Tehran’s attacks on Washington’s interests.”
For many in the region, Israel, which once pushed for the normalisation of ties with Saudi Arabia, has demonstrated post-2023 that it is more interested in settling differences using military power than negotiations.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has also begun to speak of the dangers of an emerging “Sunni axis” — though he has not defined what that might be.
Experts, however, argue his remarks could end up being a self-fulfilling prophecy that brings Sunni-majority powers together. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye all have Sunni majorities.
Iran, meanwhile, has already attacked Saudi Arabia, as have other Iranian-backed groups. Saudi Arabia, for its part, has responded with strikes on Iranian-backed groups in Iraq.
New members?
It remains unclear whether the Mecca Joint Defence Pact may still expand to include other states, such as Egypt, Qatar, Syria and the United Arab Emirates (UAE).
The benefits of such an alliance are understandable: The Middle East’s Sunni-majority countries have often been divided, with observers arguing this is the reason for their inability to deal with dangers from Israel and Iran.
But past divisions, as well as differing interests, make the expansion of the alliance a less-than-foregone conclusion.
Syria, for instance, is focused on post-war reconstruction after a brutal 13-year conflict. Its position on Israel’s northern border could make it hesitant to enter into a pact that might be perceived negatively by that country.
Egypt, likewise, has signalled its focus is on the economy and avoiding domestic upheaval.
In the past, it has hesitated to join a Saudi-led maritime alliance to protect shipping routes in the region, for fear of being dragged into a regional conflict.
The UAE could be another potential member of the Saudi-Pakistan-Turkiye alliance, but its positions have repeatedly diverged from those countries in recent years, most notably over issues like Yemen and its normalisation of ties with Israel.
The result of that normalisation, the US-backed Abraham Accords, presents another regional grouping, more aligned with Israel, that could be seen as a rival to the Mecca alliance nations.
The complicated nature of Middle East relations highlights the problems inherent in any narrative about the emergence of a new regional order following Friday’s pact.
Alliances shift in the region, going back decades. They may yet shift again.

title: Medics among six Palestinians injured in Israeli attacks across West Bank
summary: Since January, Palestinians have reported more than 11,000 Israeli attacks in the occupied West Bank, officials say.
full_text:
Medics among six Palestinians injured in Israeli attacks across West Bank
Since January, Palestinians have reported more than 11,000 Israeli attacks in the occupied West Bank, officials say.
Israeli forces and settlers have injured six Palestinians, including two paramedics, in a series of attacks across the occupied West Bank governorates of Nablus and Bethlehem, according to authorities.
The Palestine Red Crescent Society (PRCS) said its crews treated a man beaten by Israeli forces in Beit Furik, east of Nablus, on Friday. The organisation said it was coordinating with the International Committee of the Red Cross to secure access to the man, who had been arrested following the assault.

Settlers separately vandalised a Palestinian-owned vehicle in the same town, the organisation said.
In Bethlehem, three Palestinians were wounded after settlers attacked vehicles in the Abu Njeim area. Meanwhile, an ambulance crew responding to injured people in the nearby Khalayel al-Louz area was pelted with stones, injuring two paramedics and damaging the vehicle, according to the PRCS.
The Friday attacks follow a week of Israeli military raids across the occupied West Bank, including a recent two-day operation on the Qalandiya refugee camp that injured 48 people.
Palestinian monitors have documented more than 11,000 attacks across the West Bank since January.
Since October 2023, when Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza, Israeli forces and settlers have killed at least 1,182 Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, injured about 13,000 and arrested nearly 25,000, according to Palestinian officials.
Rights groups charge that the accelerated violence is aimed at deepening Israel’s illegal control over Palestinian towns and villages in the region.
The United Nations Human Rights Office (OHCHR) has said settlers, alongside Israeli forces, “frequently attack families, burn mosques and destroy and confiscate property”.
It said movement restrictions have become “tighter than ever”.
In late July, OHCHR spokesperson Ravina Shamdasani said it was imperative for countries to “bring an end to the Israeli occupation” of the West Bank.
“With attacks by Israeli settlers, and the creation of settlements and outposts hitting an all-time high, third States must act urgently and in unison to halt the continuing killing and dispossession of the Palestinian people,” she said.

title: Police officers investigated over handling of sex offender who murdered two women
summary: Simon Levy was a serial sex offender who was being monitored by police when he killed two women.
full_text:
Police officers investigated over handling of sex offender who murdered two women
- Published
Two Metropolitan Police officers are being investigated by a watchdog over alleged failures in their handling of a serial sex offender who murdered two women.
Simon Levy, 40, was on bail and being monitored by police when he committed a violent rape in January 2025, and killed Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in March of that year and Sheryl Wilkins, 39, five months later.
The Independent Office of Police Conduct (IOPC) said a police constable was under a gross misconduct investigation and a detective sergeant a misconduct investigation relating to the management of Levy.
The Met, British Transport Police, and the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) have admitted to significant shortcomings.
- How police let a registered sex offender murder and attack women 
  - Published4 hours ago
- Serial sex offender guilty of double murder and rape 
  - Published6 hours ago
Levy, from Tottenham, north London, was found guilty at the Old Bailey on Friday of two counts of murder, two counts of rape, grievous bodily harm with intent, and non-fatal suffocation.
He was remanded into custody ahead of sentencing on 12 August.
The IOPC later confirmed its investigation began in January following a voluntary conduct referral from the Metropolitan Police and remains ongoing.
It added that issuing misconduct or gross misconduct notices does not necessarily mean disciplinary proceedings will follow.
The watchdog is examining the management of Levy over a four-year period, from his first conviction in September 2021 on sexual assault charges up to his arrest in September 2025.
Levy had been released from prison on licence in February 2023 and was briefly returned to prison in May 2024 after being accused of rape and breaching his licence conditions but was not charged.
On Friday, he was convicted at the Old Bailey of two murders, rape and other charges including grievous bodily harm with intent, and non-fatal suffocation against the surviving woman.
The jury, which was given a majority direction in the trial, found him guilty on all counts.
During his trial jurors heard Levy had a string of convictions for attacking women dating back to July 2018, including one carried out against a prison officer in 2022.
An IOPC spokesperson said: "We are examining whether action could or should have been taken to prevent his reoffending, and if all officers involved in his management followed policies, procedures, and training.
"We are also assessing whether any learning, whether individual, force-wide, or nationally, or other changes should be implemented in light of the events under investigation."
Speaking outside court on Friday, Det Ch Insp Neil John, who led the investigation, said Trujillo and Wilkins were "much-loved women" and praised their families for demonstrating "incredible dignity and remarkable resolve".
John also praised the surviving victim for her "commendable bravery" in presenting "vital evidence" in court before appealing directly for any further victims to come forward.
"Although we are proud of the work that has gone into securing this verdict, we remain relentless in pursuing offenders who perpetrate violence against women and girls and are appealing to anyone who is yet to report offences relating to Levy to come forward," he added.
Assistant Chief Constable Charlie Doyle of British Transport Police also encouraged any potential survivors to step forward.
Met Deputy Assistant Commissioner Kevin Southworth has acknowledged that failures to remand Levy in custody during court hearings in May and June 2025 left him free to commit further offences.
BTP confirmed two officers have been moved to other roles due to "incompetence" in handling investigations into Levy's transport assaults.
Crime and policing minister Sarah Jones said the situation "raises serious questions".
"The fact that Levy was able to inflict such devastating harm after being freed by police and the courts is deeply concerning."
Lisa Ramsarran, chief crown prosecutor for the CPS, said: "Our actions fell short of the standards that victims, families and the public are entitled to expect.
"In particular, there were points where we could and should have taken a more robust approach to representations about bail, based on the information available."

title: Fifth heatwave of the year likely next week as temperatures could hit 35C
summary: As temperatures start to rise again over the weekend, many parts of England and Wales will enter into the fifth heatwave of the year, as Simon King explains
full_text:
Fifth heatwave of the year likely next week as temperatures could hit 35C
- Published
Heat will once again build across the UK this weekend before the fifth widespread heatwave of the year is likely to be declared next week.
From Sunday and into next week, temperatures could exceed 30C in south-east England.
Yellow heat health alerts have been issued for most of England until Tuesday, warning of impacts for health and social care services and an increased risk to life for vulnerable people.
These are likely to be updated by the UK Health Security Agency in the coming days as a widespread heatwave develops.
How hot will it get?
Temperatures on Saturday will begin to climb above average again, reaching the mid- to high 20s Celsius in most of England and Wales.
It will be cooler in Scotland and Northern Ireland at 17 to 21C with more cloud, a bit of rain and a blustery wind.
By Sunday and into next week temperatures will rise even further with many parts of the UK exceeding their heatwave threshold temperature of 25 to 28C, depending on location.
With this hotter weather expected to last well into the week, many locations will have the three consecutive days needed to declare the fifth widespread heatwave of the year.
It has already been a remarkable summer in the United Kingdom with multiple records broken.
July has been the sunniest month on record for the UK, as well as the driest July on record for England and Wales.
There have so far been 33 days this year when temperatures have exceeded 30C in the UK. Next week, it is likely the record of 34 days, set in 1995, will be broken.
For the first time ever, a temperature of 35C has also been recorded somewhere in the UK on the three consecutive months of May, June and July.
It is possible August will join that list by the end of next week as some forecast models suggest 35C in central and south-east England.
No significant rain in sight
Some rain is forecast for Scotland and Northern Ireland on Saturday before reaching northern England and north Wales on Sunday; elsewhere, it is likely to remain dry.
Wisley in Surrey is now up to 51 days without recording any rain.
This could easily rise to 60 days with no rain the forecast across southern England.
Despite the ongoing dry weather, August is typically the wettest of the summer months across the UK.
There are signs that the second half of the month could become unsettled as low pressure becomes more dominant.
However, with no significant rain in sight across England and Wales, the current drought conditions with hosepipe bans will show now sign of easing.

title: 'I ran because I knew I would die': Russian drones target medics in Ukraine
summary: Ukrainian emergency workers warn of growing Russian attacks on hospitals and ambulances.
full_text:
'I ran because I knew I would die': Russian drones target medics in Ukraine
- Published
Inna Lytvynenko always puts on her bright orange body armour when she's out on an emergency call.
Last June, the paramedic was sent out in Kherson to treat a woman injured in a Russian drone attack, when an FPV drone smashed into her ambulance.
Seconds later, she heard a buzzing sound in the sky. Another drone was flying straight towards her, fast.
"I panicked. I grabbed my trauma bag and started running," she recalls. "I shouted and screamed. I knew that if I stopped, I would die."
After chasing her for about 10 minutes, the drone flew away. Lytvynenko was quickly picked up by police.
But what she called the "safari hunting" continued. Drones hit two more vehicles that arrived to take the injured woman to hospital. Hours later, a third police car finally managed to get her out.
After another "safari" attack earlier this week, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called to put greater pressure on Russia in order to stop deliberate "hunting attacks" on civilians.
Hospitals and ambulances in Ukraine are increasingly coming under Russian drone and missile attack, even though, according to the international rules of war known as the Geneva Conventions, they must be protected by all parties to the conflict.
"This is a new normality, which should not be the normality," says Dr Jarno Habicht, the World Health Organization's (WHO) representative in Ukraine.
The WHO has registered 3,118 attacks on healthcare since the start of the Russian invasion in February 2022. "That's two cases per day," Habicht says.
Since 2023 the number of attacks on healthcare has steadily grown. In 2024 it went up by 30%. Last year there was another 20% increase. This trend is expected to continue this year.
A recent Doctors Without Borders (MSF) report, external says that Russia systematically and often deliberately targets Ukrainian medical facilities. The frequency of attacks on healthcare suggests that they are "a sustained feature of the war rather than an episodic consequence of large scale offensives," the report said.
Last month Russian missiles hit a hospital in Kherson, badly damaging the building and killing one doctor.
Hospital director Olena Tymoshenko believes it was a targeted attack. "It wasn't just one missile, there were three missiles that hit the hospital within a few minutes from each other. It cannot be an accident," she told the BBC.
Moscow also often uses a "double-tap" tactic, when they target the same location twice within a short period of time. Many believe that the second attack is deliberately aimed at first responders who arrive at the scene of the initial strike to rescue survivors.
During a recent massive Russian air attack on Kyiv, seven people were killed, including a police officer and a volunteer, after a second strike on the same location.
And lately Russian forces have been also targeting warehouses of humanitarian organisations. Last month alone, warehouses of three UN agencies, including the WHO, were damaged during air strikes. According to Habicht, the organisation shares coordinates of its facilities with both Moscow and Kyiv specifically in order to protect them from strikes.
While missile and drone strikes can be indiscriminate, first-person view (FPV) drone strikes are almost always intentional. A drone pilot can see the target in a live feed from the drone's camera. So when it hits an ambulance, it has to be on purpose, says Robin Meldrum, MSF country coordinator in Ukraine.
Dr Inna Lytvynenko says that she was wearing a uniform identifying her as a medical worker. The ambulance was also clearly marked. So, she believes the drone operator consciously chose to target them.
According to the WHO, strikes on ambulances make up 20% of all attacks on Ukraine's healthcare system, which suggests these are part of a calculated strategy.
The result of such sustained attacks is that the civilian population close to the frontline are getting increasingly cut off from health services.
The majority of people left in these areas are elderly people who often chronic diseases. Even if they survive air strikes and shelling, without medication and occasional check-ups they face a slow death.
And ambulances may not be able to reach them if the risks are high.
Lytvynenko and her colleagues constantly monitor social media to learn about threats.
"It's really scary," she says. "Every time when we take a patient to hospital, we just pray. These drones can appear from anywhere, they can even get through anti-drone nets."
In some cases, police are dispatched instead of ambulances.
Since the danger zone where FPV drones operate is growing – as both Ukraine and Russia develop drones with greater and greater ranges – mobile clinics run by various health organisations have had to shift their operations further and further away from the frontline.
"Two years ago, we could go up to 5-8km (3.1-5 miles) from the frontline," says Meldrum. "Now we won't go anywhere within 30km and this distance keeps growing."
Over the past 18 months, MSF stopped regular visits to about 80 villages near the front where they had provided health services, says Meldrum. And recently it has paused ambulance services in Sloviansk, a major city in eastern Ukraine.
"It doesn't feel like we're protected in this environment, and in the way that Russia is conducting the war," Meldrum says.
"We don't feel that the rules of war are being respected."

title: Book hidden in fireplace returned to Australian library 150 years overdue
summary: It is thought an apprentice stonemason who worked on the Houses of Parliament in London borrowed it.
full_text:
Book hidden in fireplace returned to Australian library 150 years overdue
- Published
A book borrowed 150 years ago has finally been returned to an Australian library, with the culprit linked to the Houses of Parliament in London.
Antiquities of Athens was borrowed from a local library in Kiama, a seaside town about 120km (75 miles) south of Sydney, some time in the mid-1870s.
The book on classic Greek architecture was stored in a tea chest hidden behind a boarded-up fireplace for decades before it was recently discovered by a family member.
Ross Simmons, 77, thinks his great-grandfather, John Simmons, might have borrowed the book to help with his career, having worked as an apprentice stonemason in Westminster in the mid-1800s before becoming an architect in Australia.
Simmons, a self-confessed family history buff, said his great-grandfather studied in London between 1839 to 1844.
"After his studies in London, he was apprenticed to other stonemasons to help in the construction of the Houses of Parliament," Simmons said.
In 1857, aged 27, John Simmons emigrated from the UK to Australia, first living in the Sydney suburb of Newtown before relocating to Kiama after leading the construction of a sandstone church in the coastal town.
"He had quite an interest in architecture, construction and building," Simmons said, adding that the overdue book "probably sat on a shelf at his house" and was used as a reference.
The book somehow ended up in a tea chest - along with other family records - which was placed in a fireplace that was covered up.
About 30 years ago, the tea chest was uncovered during renovations and the books - including the overdue one - were given to Simmons for safekeeping.
But it wasn't until about a fortnight ago that he went through some of the books in greater detail.
"I looked inside the front cover and, lo and behold, on the second page there was a Kiama Library stamp," Simmons said, with the library's borrowing conditions also detailed on the inside cover.
For instance, library members could only borrow one book at a time, unless it could be proved that six people in the same household could read, in which case, three books could be lent out.
Anyone intoxicated was barred from borrowing and members returning books past their due date would be fined three pence for every week it was late.
Kiama Library staff worked out that the fine would be £97 - or in today's currency AU$28,000 ($20,000; £15,000), allowing for inflation. But luckily for the Simmons family, the fine has been waived.
Kiama Council libraries manager Michelle Hudson said the unusual find had attracted a lot of attention.
"People have travelled 40 minutes away to come and actually hold the book... it's a beautiful little book and it's got an amazing story to tell," she said.
The cloth-bound volume has some water damage but otherwise, is in good condition, Hudson said.
"It does have beautiful illustrations in it and some pages that fold out to show you they were using exact measurements of some of the monuments in Greece."
She said in 1872, the council got a £200 grant to establish the town's library and and it had fewer than 1,000 books in its collection, with the overdue book marked as number 506.
There's no way to know exactly who borrowed the book or when, Hudson said, as the library's borrowing records from that period have since been lost.
However, the book is no longer available to borrow, having been added to the library's collection of special items, which can be viewed on request.
"It won't be able to go out again... we don't want to wait another 150 years for it to come back," Hudson joked.
As for the book's much-delayed return, Simmons said he believes his great-grandfather would be pleased with the final chapter of its journey.
"I think he'd be happy to see the book returned and he'd probably have a bit of a laugh about it."

title: I went for a full body MOT and the results came as a shock
summary: The private body scan industry is booming, but is it doing more harm than good?
full_text:
I went for a full body MOT and the results came as a shock
- Published
I don't mind having my photo taken - triple checked and filtered for Instagram - but 70 cameras pointing at me while I'm down to my knickers is a bit daunting.
A robotic voice tells me to stay still and close my eyes as I stand in a huge curved scanner while classical music plays in the background.
With a flash of light, 2,000 photographs are taken of my body, in the hope of capturing every mark, freckle and mole to analyse for different skin cancers.
This full-body scan is happening at a sci-fi-style clinic in Manchester city centre, with me wearing a dressing gown and hexagon-shaped rubber slippers. The millions of data points collected will create a 3D avatar of my body using AI.
Over the past two years, the market for health MOTs has boomed, with people willing to pay hundreds, or even thousands, for them, and companies such as Prenuvo, Ezra and Neko Health raising millions in venture capital.
While Prenuvo and Ezra offer a whole-body MRI scan, I've opted for Neko Health, which doesn't delve quite as deeply, and comes with a more modest £299 price tag. There are currently 100,000 people on its waiting list.
I will be screened for a range of different conditions, including skin cancer, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, eye conditions like glaucoma, as well as kidney and blood disorders.
I don't have any symptoms, but what if they do find something? More on that later.
The body scan industry sees itself as a new frontier in healthcare, preventing disease before it has a chance to fully appear. But there is scepticism about how beneficial these scans really are for otherwise healthy patients.
My socials are inundated with videos of enthusiastic clients filming themselves in scan machines, getting their bloods taken and testing their grip strength.
Hjalmar Nilsonne, one of the founders of Neko Health, wants to see this preventative treatment available for every individual, not just those who can afford to pay for it.
"While medicine has progressed so much over the past century, primary care is still very basic. Why wait until we see symptoms?" Nilsonne says. "The data is super clear - prevention is preferable to cure."
However, GPs and doctors in the wider NHS are more sceptical, with NHS England warning that the popularity of these scans is leading to more "over-diagnosis, unnecessary investigations and avoidable anxiety".
As well as having a scan myself, I've spoken to two women who had very different experiences.
'My cancerous skin marks were missed'
Annabel Mason-Thompson went for a Neko Health scan in September last year, knowing she had a suspicious-looking mark on her back - but it wasn't flagged by the technology.
"I felt a bit let down if I'm honest," the 50-year-old says. "Their AI scanner failed to pick up any of my four cancerous lesions.
"It was only when I went into the doctor's room after the scan and I pointed out my red mark did they take a look at it."
Further examination confirmed the mark was suspicious, so Neko Health contacted Annabel to say she would need treatment and wrote a letter to her private dermatologist to say the "lesion requires evaluation with a view to possible excision".
Her dermatologist found three more cancerous marks which needed urgent treatment.
"Luckily," she says, "they were all slow-growing basal cell carcinomas. I had to have two cut out and two taken off via cryotherapy."
Neko Health says "member safety and clinical excellence are at the heart of everything" it does. The company said its clinical team did identify a "lesion of concern" and it was reviewed by two of its dermatologists before a referral was made for potential treatment.
"We know that no one system is foolproof," Nilsonne says, "which is why we have multiple lenses - it is crucial that the technology and human expertise work together."
His company's latest data shows that of the 4,362 scans carried out on clients who visited Neko Health's Stockholm headquarters last year, 1.2% discovered life-threatening conditions such as melanoma and leukaemia. A further 4% spotted significant health conditions that required further treatment, and 1.2% flagged conditions that could be reversed such as pre-diabetic blood sugar levels.
While the figures are not representative of the population and only account for those who can afford to pay for this kind of preventive healthcare, Nilsonne says this is an indicator of how medicine should look in the future.
But GPs disagree. Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs (RCGP), says they haven't seen "convincing evidence" private broad screening tests "improve health outcomes".
She says the results from these private scans can also place an additional strain on the NHS as clients come back for further tests and potential treatment, even "where the findings prove to be clinically insignificant".
'It saved my life'
Mehvish says nothing could have prepared her for what she was told after her full body scan. She left Birmingham's Neko Health clinic with a life-changing diagnosis.
"I expected to feel relief," the 33-year-old says. "Instead, I was told that I had a rare form of diabetes."
After her long-term blood sugar levels came back very high, she had another blood test which confirmed she had suspected diabetes.
She was referred back to her GP, who sent her for an urgent hospital appointment the same day, and was diagnosed with Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA), a type of diabetes which bridges both type 1 and type 2.
Like type 1, it is an autoimmune condition that attacks the body's pancreatic cells, but it also shares traits with type 2 because it can progress slowly and, depending on the stage of the condition, it can initially be managed with diet and exercise.
"I didn't have any of the symptoms," Mehvish says, "It was difficult to get my head round it - how could I have this condition and not know about it?"
But she says the early, unexpected intervention "saved my life".
Now she injects insulin twice a day, monitors what she eats, and despite missing the spontaneity of her old life, is learning to adapt to her new one.
"I feel so much better, more clarity, less brain fog and I feel so much more balanced."
After my own scan, I'm feeling slightly out of balance. I've been told I have 3,311 skin markings - compared to the average Neko Health client's 845. Three need extra review by the company's dermatologist in Sweden.
"But I don't have any big moles or markings," I say during the post-scan consultation with a doctor. It's my freckles, I'm told, and having freckles puts me at higher risk of skin cancer.
Having felt confident I would get a clean bill of health - especially when it comes to my skin - I was a bit unnerved to discover that I'd need to have extra tests.
As well as the three suspicious-looking moles that needed further attention, I also discovered I have an unusual heart rate. The trace from the electrocardiogram (ECG) highlighted an extra wave, known as a bifid P wave, which was referred to Neko Health's in-house cardiologist for review. Thankfully, it came back all clear.
A few days later, I received a follow-up text to say there were no abnormal skin changes that required treatment.
I am one of thousands of clients who has had something flagged as a potential issue, then later found no further treatment was required. Some doctors say this causes unnecessary anxiety and that patients should only rely on national screening programmes through the NHS.
Dr Stephen Harden, president of the Royal Society of Radiologists, points to the technology used in the NHS, which targets "specific areas" like the breasts, bowel or cervix, and which he says may be more reliable than a whole-body scan.
But former health minister Steve Brine says precautionary scans like the one I had "fit the direction of travel of how people are approaching their health".

title: How a former GB Olympian curbed his porn problem - and the signs and steps to recovery
summary: Experts share the signs to look out for if you are worried about your porn use, and how to seek help.
full_text:
How a former GB Olympian curbed his porn problem - and the signs and steps to recovery
- Published
Former Team GB diver Freddie Woodward was a teenager when he realised he had a problem with porn.
"Every time I sat down to revise, all I wanted to do was open those sites," he revealed.
By age 12, he was regularly visiting what he calls "hardcore" sites. As his career progressed - which included representing his country in the Olympics - he was watching adult content several times a day.
Now aged 30, the Olympian has told the BBC how he eventually curbed his habit by shifting his mindset.
"You can't be the person who is trying to quit porn. You have to be someone who doesn't watch porn, and that takes a lot of work," he said.
So how can you spot when a porn habit has become unhealthy, and how can you tackle it?
Although it has become a common phrase, "porn addiction" is not an officially recognised condition in its own right.
"We know a lot of people have a problem with porn," explains sex and relationship psychotherapist Silva Neves, who says the matter has become more prevalent among clients at his private practice.
But experts are divided as to whether it is a true "addiction" – like someone might experience with drugs, for example – and how best to deal with it.
Researcher Campbell Ince, from Australia's Monash University, says the vast majority of clinicians now agree people can suffer from "problematic porn use", but there is still a lot to figure out about its causes and treatments.
This means there is no definitive list of symptoms or treatments available to those worried they may be addicted.
Some clinicians approach it as a compulsive sexual behaviour disorder, a condition recognised by the World Health Organization.
This is sexual behaviour that "feels out of control, is causing significant distress, and despite repeated attempts to control it, they can't," explains psychotherapist Dr Paula Hall, who works privately at the Laurel Centre, a sex and porn addiction centre, and also runs a not-for-profit service.
The NHS does say, external it is possible to be addicted to "just about anything", including sex.
'I didn't know how to get it to loosen its grip on me'
So what are the markers of an unhealthy porn habit? Neves says it's "not about the frequency or duration, it's about the damage to your life".
That might be arriving late to work because you were up all night watching porn, prioritising it above commitments to your loved ones, or watching it in the office, he says.
Other crucial questions to ask yourself are whether you can actually cut back or adjust your habit when you try, and whether you carry on watching despite enjoying it less and less, adds Ince, whose research focuses on problematic porn use.
For Craig, who describes himself as a recovering addict, it was this loss of control which marked a turning point during the Covid-19 pandemic, when he was in his mid-thirties.
"I don't think it ever became a huge issue for me until lockdown, where that extra pressure, extra isolation, just compounded the issue.
"I didn't know how to get it to loosen its grip on me," he recalls.
Ince cautions that many people may feel distress about their porn use for social, moral or religious reasons – but that this does not necessarily mean your habit is out of control.
"Someone could be watching porn for five minutes, three times a week – and because they have a lot of shame, they think 'I'm an addict'," agrees Neves.
"But then there might be someone who watches it every day and thinks it's fine."
Hall similarly encourages clients to "get away from the idea of 'I'm either an addict or I'm not'", and focus instead on how much it is affecting things like your studies and relationships.
TV presenter Ore Oduba last year spoke publicly about his 30-year-long porn addiction which began at the age of nine – saying it had been "destroying my life from the inside out".
"It was the thing from a very early age that I was running to as a response to a lot of trauma", he told the We Need to Talk podcast last year, before curbing the habit.
- 'I couldn’t stop watching': Personal stories of how porn obsession takes over lives 
  - Published29 November 2024
- Can you be addicted to sex? 
  - Published6 May 2018
It is not clear what might cause such behaviour, as experts say much more research is needed.
"The scientific examination is certainly accelerating, but there is a very long way to go," Ince says.
It might begin as something which gives you a break from other issues in your life, says Hall, such as a stressful career or relationship breakdown.
There may also be "predisposing factors", such as trauma, issues from early childhood, or negative self-belief, that can make it harder to curb your use, she says.
Craig, now 40, says porn became a "tool to turn to for every one of life's ups and downs".
He remembers feeling he was "broken, that there was no way out", before recovery helped him to think differently.
Hall also points to the impact of the digital environment and people becoming "addicted by design" through algorithms.
Both she and Neves say AI-generated porn is making matters worse by enabling people to create "exactly what they want and need", as Neves describes it.
'It's one day at a time'
If you are worried about your porn use, Ince recommends seeking out support from a qualified and experienced professional.
A registered psychologist can be particularly helpful because they may consider your mental health more broadly, "and we know that co-occurring mental health problems are more or less the rule, rather than the exception", he says.
This was the case for Craig, who did not realise his porn use may be unhealthy until he started therapy for his mental health.
"Porn addiction was like a contributing factor," he came to learn.
His therapist suggested he join a 12-step programme for sex addiction – a recovery model created by Alcoholics Anonymous – which he credits for his recovery.
"I didn't necessarily find it easy and straightforward to step away from my addiction. I feel I'm in a good place now, but also acknowledge the fact it's one day at a time."
There is currently no central, dedicated NHS service for those struggling with their porn use – although some local services offer support, and you can talk to your GP. This means treatment will more likely come from private practitioners, support groups or online self-help.
Ince suggests doing thorough research to find the right fit for you, and cautions against using online resources which may offer generic advice.
Some practitioners will help clients towards cutting out porn altogether, while others will help people "integrate it into their lives in a way that is functional," says Neves.
Seeking to understand any underlying factors will be a crucial part of treatment, says Hall.
There are some practical steps you can take yourself, she says, such as placing blocking software on your device.
She also advises recognising when you might feel more susceptible to using porn – which, for some, can be when you are stressed or alone – and planning ahead for what you might do instead.
But she says there should ultimately be more support on the NHS, particularly early intervention before porn can take over a person's life.
A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Social Care said: "It is troubling to hear accounts of individuals becoming addicted to pornography at such a young age.
"It reinforces the importance of the online safety laws we have put in place to prevent children from accessing harmful content."

title: Digital cameras and wired earphones are back - and 'a bit more real'
summary: We're surrounded by more advanced tech in 2026, so why are young people going back to basics?
full_text:
Digital cameras and wired earphones are back - and 'a bit more real'
- Published
It's Saturday afternoon and I've nearly fallen at the first hurdle – I've left my digital camera battery on charge at home.
Forgive me, I last took this camera out with me 15 years ago on a family holiday to the Canary Islands.
Take two. Now with the charged battery in hand, I'm taking my digital camera to a DJ set as an experiment.
It's because older technology is having a bit of a moment – social media is full of people talking about why they're going back to basics with the likes of digital cameras, wired headphones and early MP3 players.
Sales of iPods and Walkman portable audio players in the UK on eBay increased by nearly 50% in 2025, the online marketplace told us, while searches for iPod minis on the platform have increased by 48% over the last year.
Digital cameras - smoother than phone pics?
Luckily I'm out with my photography-loving best friend, who helps adjust the settings on the camera and gets snapping while I'm otherwise engaged on the dancefloor.
The mere sight of us pulling out the camera and squinting through its tiny viewfinder draws attention – "I've not seen one of these in years", a man remarks.
He's right – digital cameras had their heyday in the late 1990s and early 2000s, just before smartphones took off.
There are currently 42 million active film camera users globally, more than a third of these aged 18–30 and largely influenced by social media trends, according to a market research report, external last year.
So why, when we're surrounded by more advanced tech here in 2026, are they seemingly making a resurgence?
For Lily Redman, a 26-year-old content creator from South Wales, digital cameras "capture a quality that my phone just can't replicate".
She's been taking one on nights out and to concerts and feels the flash on her phone "is grainy and too high definition" compared to the "more smooth" finished product on a digital camera.
"I think people are looking for a bit of grit or something that feels a bit more real," she says.
That may also explain why low exposure photos taken on iPhones and Androids – where people dodge ready-made filters to artificially crank down the exposure setting and produce a darker image – are also popular on socials right now.
With digital cameras offering an element of surprise when you plug in the memory card reader to your computer at home, digital cameras capture a moment in time.
"If I look back at photos my mum took when I was two, they look so old but when I look at photos I took five years ago, they look like they were taken yesterday," says Redman.
"Phone photos have warped our perception of time."
Early MP3 devices - a reminder of 'simpler times'
It's not just digital cameras returning from the archives (or a dusty cupboard), but early MP3 devices like iPods too.
According to refurbished tech website Backmarket, iPods are "driving the trend" in sales of older MP3 devices with a 48% increase in sales between 2024 and 2025, with demand for MP3 and MP4 players "accelerating further into 2026".
Cheri Sanih, 30, runs a Tumblr account about older technology which she says has gained thousands of followers recently.
As she scrolls through the music library on her mint green iPod, filled with album artwork from 15 to 20 years ago, childhood memories of receiving one as a Christmas present come flooding back.
For her, it's all about nostalgically "wanting to remember simpler times"; being able to "bury into escapism".
Sanih points out how her "phone is always getting notifications and sometimes I just want to be outside, blissfully listening to music".
She thinks iPods have become popular again because of their "beautiful design" and the way the music player is "the first bit of technology really catering to humans with a less cluttered user interface".
Move over bluetooth, we're wired
And speaking of back to basics, wired headphones are perhaps as simple as you can get, but again proving popular online.
These are now a daily staple for 23-year-old Monique Wellman-Mason from Bristol, who grew tired of losing her wireless earbuds.
"Every single time I get them out my bag I spend two minutes trying to detangle them which is a bit of a pain," she jokes, "but at the same time I love that they have a microphone and I'm [always] connected to my phone".
She tells the BBC that the clear mic is useful for her job as a social media manager and she enjoys being able to "spark that nostalgia", while another positive is wired earphones are "really cheap" at about £20.
Monique made the switch from bluetooth wireless to wired earphones a few months back and says she hasn't returned to the former since.
"Technology only goes up and we're always looking for the quickest thing but this is a step back in a way – I love it," she says.
Whether it's digital cameras, iPods or wired earphones, does a renewed love for early-digital gadgets among some young people tell us something more?
It's been on the mind of Andrew Przybylski, professor of technology and human behaviour at the University of Oxford.
Underpinning a fondness for more basic tech is "people's desire on a very deep level to be in control of their experiences," he argues.
He says the modern digital world often leaves us inflicted by decision paralysis, external - the inability to choose because there are so many options.
When a new series comes out, he explains, "binge watching it automatically" often feels like a decision that is made for us.
In contrast, when you choose to turn on a digital camera and play with its settings or add an album to your iPod library "you move towards something you want versus it coming at you".
Andrew says "people want more than to just rent the things [and experiences] they're passionate about" and that buying your own music or taking your own pictures creates a sense of connection.
He references Xbox's server outage in late July, in which users couldn't play games even if they owned the discs and how "nobody liked that".
"Imagine if a book worked that way," he adds.
Additional reporting by Amy Walker.

title: The phone book that led us to Assad's spy chief in hiding
summary: How we tracked down "The Spider" who was once one of the most-feared men in Syria.
full_text:
The phone book that led us to Assad's spy chief in hiding
- Published
In an abandoned luxury apartment in the Syrian capital Damascus, armed men dressed in military fatigues sifted through designer clothes and documents.
Scattered across the living room floor, under a sparkling crystal chandelier, were dozens of photos of the same slender man in different settings - sitting at his desk, even playing in the snow. And multiple prints of the same image, showing him smiling warmly as he shook the hand of ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad.
The man was not instantly recognisable, but gold medals and gilded certificates piled nearby were inscribed with the name Hussam Luka.
Known as "The Spider", Luka was one of Assad's top henchmen, accused of orchestrating atrocities and systematic torture, and sanctioned by the UK, US and European Union.
As head of Syria's most powerful civilian intelligence agency, Luka was among the most feared men in the country. But much of his work was conducted from the shadows.
Like others in the regime, Luka seemingly vanished overnight in December 2024 when Assad was toppled, leaving a trail of unanswered questions and demands for justice that many fear will never be realised.
In his apartment, days after Assad's fall, we watched the rebels looking for clues as to where he might have gone.
In the corner of the living room, on a console table, was an unremarkable-looking notebook.
Inside, in scribbled blue handwriting, we found dozens of names - from shopkeepers and doctors, to military officials and people with the Luka family name.
Could these contacts help us learn more about The Spider and his crimes, or even help us to track him down?
At one time, Luka's own phone number was hard to avoid - in the early days of the Syrian civil war, it had been spray-painted on walls around the central city of Homs.
The conflict was sparked by Assad's brutal crushing of a pro-democracy uprising in 2011 - a war in which hundreds of thousands of people would go on to be killed.
Luka was a local head of the Political Security Directorate, one of Assad's main intelligence agencies, and had been given the task of wresting the city from the rebels.
At the time, rebel-held areas in Homs were under siege by the government, and residents were struggling to access food and medicine. Several people, including former rebel fighter Motaz al-Zaydi, told us they had resorted to eating rats.
Al-Zaydi remembers Luka's name and phone number appearing on a wall in his neighbourhood, and said the message began to spread that those wanting to flee the fighting could phone the number for safe passage.
Some are believed to have been granted safe transit out of the city by Luka, but others who called the number were never seen or heard from again, according to several people we spoke to, including al-Zaydi.
Many told us they referred to Luka as "The Spider" because of his vast web of allies and informants, including some embedded in rebel groups. "He was everywhere," Homs residents told us. Al-Zaydi described Luka as an "evil genius" and "a fox of a man".
But his most egregious action in the city, many argue, was his alleged involvement in the so-called Eid Massacre, known by some as the Children's Massacre, which the US noted when sanctioning him.
It was the Muslim holiday of Eid al-Adha in September 2015, and Mohammed Towakatli's seven-year-old, Wael, was gardening in the playground he had set up in the al-Waer neighbourhood.
At 17:10, just after the power ration had kicked in, Mohammed remembers the strike hitting.
As Mohammed walked around the park earlier this year, now planted with rows of saplings, he recalled the names of the children killed and the games they had been playing at the time, gesturing to the places where he had found their bodies, including that of Wael.
"They were tiny children," he said with tears in his eyes. "The ground here was painted red with blood."
Twenty-eight people were killed, including 17 children and four women, according to the Syrian Network for Human Rights.
Luka, according to a Syrian activist group, and a pro-opposition newspaper at the time, was responsible for the regime's selection of targets in the area that day.
His actions in Homs earned him a promotion, and by the time of the regime's collapse he ran the General Security Directorate (GSD) intelligence agency, making him one of the most powerful people in the country.
The government security services could target anyone - from opposition fighters, journalists, doctors, or rights activists, to people believed to be opposed in any form to the Assad government.
Those arrested were detained in Syria's political prisons, including Sednaya in Damascus - a facility so notorious it was dubbed the "human slaughterhouse". Many imprisoned there were never seen again.
As head of the GSD, Luka had strategic control over Syria's detention policies, and his personnel would monitor communications to and from Sednaya.
There are widespread calls across Syrian society on social media for former senior officials to be held accountable. Some also say the new Syrian government is not doing enough to bring these people to justice.
Syria's Attorney General, Hassan al-Turba, told the BBC the government had launched a lawsuit against Luka, accusing him of "premeditated murder, torture, and death resulting from torture".
"A warrant has been circulated domestically and we are working on circulating it internationally as well," he said, adding the administration was working to track the location and seek the extradition of Luka and other missing senior regime officials.
As he continues to grieve for his son, Mohammed told the BBC he wanted Luka, alongside other senior regime officials, to be returned to Syria and executed.
"They look like humans but have no humanity in them at all," he said.
We had taken photos of every page of the book we discovered in Luka's apartment and, back in London, began testing every one of its 155 numbers - aware that many people close to the regime would have fled or gone to ground. Fifty-one numbers appeared to be operational.
We then called these again in order of their apparent importance to Luka, starting with military commanders and relatives.
Every call was unsuccessful. Anyone who answered simply hung up when we explained who we were and what we wanted - or denied knowing Luka or his family, or even being the people listed in the book.
So a BBC reporter, whose own name was once on a GSD wanted list while Luka ran the agency, headed to Syria to try in person.
Many of those listed in the phone book were doctors, so our reporter began booking medical appointments with some of them as a way to meet them.
A doctor in Aleppo reluctantly acknowledged he had treated Luka, but then ordered our journalist to leave and returned his consultation fee.
Our reporter then booked an appointment with another doctor in the phone book, this time based in Damascus. This doctor revealed he had once accompanied Luka's mother on a medical trip to Russia, but was reluctant to give us any more information, other than to vaguely direct us to a pharmacy belonging to one of Luka's daughters.
Locals said she, too, had not been seen since December 2024.
For months we drew a blank in our hunt for Luka.
And then we had our first breakthrough.
One of those listed in the book, who we tried calling again, finally answered the phone.
He had been the guard for Luka's apartment block, he told us, and eventually agreed to give us the number for someone he said had been Luka's personal bodyguard - a man we are calling Mahmoud.
It took weeks to secure an interview with Mahmoud. Meetings would be scheduled but he would not show up, or he would request a meeting in a private space such as a car or apartment, which our reporter judged too much of a risk.
They eventually met at a hotel one night, just before midnight. Broad-shouldered and physically imposing, Mahmoud seemed to be considering every answer

title: He's been frozen on Everest for 30 years, now 'Green Boots' may finally be coming home
summary: For decades, an Indian man's lime shoes have been a grim trail marker for many climbing the world's highest peak.
full_text:
He's been frozen on Everest for 30 years, now 'Green Boots' may finally be coming home
- Published
For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit.
The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since.
Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body – arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain.
They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home.
"On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC.
"When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'"
Disaster struck on descent
The night before he left to be part of a historic Indian expedition on Everest, Morup sat with his wife at his home in Ladakh, an Indian-administered territory in another part of the Himalayas.
He made her a promise: that he would come back a hero and make his country proud.
"He asked me to take care of the kids and come to the airport to greet him on his return," Konchak Yangskit told the BBC at her home.
A lance naik, or lance corporal, in the Indo Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), the force guarding much of India's border with China, 48-year-old Morup was no stranger to Himalayan trekking.
But Yangskit says she had a strange sense of foreboding that night: "I wondered if I was ever going to see him again."
Morup was one of six climbers on the ITBP expedition attempting to reach the top of Everest – which lies on the border between Nepal and the Chinese-governed territory of Tibet.
Most climbers choose to ascend from the Nepalese side, but Morup's crew wanted to write their names into the history books as the first Indian expedition to do it from the treacherous Chinese side.
Three out of six members of the expedition turned back due to a snowstorm, but Morup and two others - Tsewang Smanla and Tsewang Paljor – kept struggling, all the way up to the 8,849m summit.
Disaster, a blizzard, struck as they descended and killed all three.
Like many of the more than 300 people who have died in the Everest region since records began a century ago, their bodies remain on the mountain.
Two have never been found, but the third body - that of "Green Boots" - has been lying frozen in the snow for three decades at an altitude of 8,500 metres.
For years, it was assumed that "Green Boots" was another member of the expedition, Tsewang Paljor.
But testimony from surviving members of the 1996 expedition and the location of the last radio contact with the climbers have now led authorities to believe the remains belong to Morup.
An ITBP official, speaking anonymously because he is not authorised to speak to the media, told BBC News Hindi that Morup's clothes and climbing gear helped officials identify the body in recent years.
Since then, they've been plotting how to get their comrade home so they can confirm his identity beyond doubt through DNA testing and offer his family a semblance of closure.
"We never forgot him. It was only a matter of time," the ITBP official said.
How difficult will it be to recover the body?
Retrieving those who have died on the mountain is a dangerous, gruelling task, and, up until the past decade, very rare.
Many of the bodies, like Morup's, are in what climbers call Everest's death zone – where temperatures can plunge to -40C and oxygen levels are about a third of those at sea level.
"The weather and snow conditions are going to be crucial," said Tshiring Jangbu Sherpa, a prominent Nepalese mountaineer who has taken part in other recovery missions.
"The north side has fewer crevasses, but it is riskier. If something bad happens from the Nepalese side, you get quickly evacuated by helicopter. But there is no such system from the Chinese side," he told BBC Hindi.
The Chinese side of the peak – where Green Boots' body is – is steeper and doesn't have the same support structures as the southern slope, which is another complicating factor, Sherpa sources have told BBC News Nepali.
"It's really tough to get that body down even in popular spring season, let alone the autumn [which has more unpredictable weather]. That's the simple reason it is still there for so many years," mountaineering guide Pemba Ongchu Sherpa said.
"There would need to be 10 to 12 climbers who are capable of making summits, just to fix [support] ropes to reach that point."
Green Boots will also have to be physically carried down to an altitude where it can be collected by a helicopter, or possibly yaks, and transported back to an airport – a job which also requires huge manpower.
Sherpas say bodies shrouded in iced-up climbing gear often weigh several times the average man and are frequently frozen into awkward positions, making bringing them down the challenging terrain even more treacherous. The remains may also begin defrosting and decomposing once they reach lower altitudes.
The start of the descent with the body would be the most difficult, Indian climber Kuntal Joisher told BBC Nepali.
"It's going to be very, very risky endeavour. It's extremely steep ground with lots of rock. Logistically, this [first] 1000m is going to be a humungous challenge."
"The main thing is to not put Sherpa lives at risk for a dead body."
All of this makes for a hugely expensive recovery mission – experts say even the most straightforward ones cost between $40,000 and $80,000, a sum beyond the means of most families.
It is more common for local teams to move people who have died out of view on the mountain: like explorer Francys Arsentiev, dubbed the Sleeping Beauty of Everest, who in 2007 was moved to a more private final resting place on Everest almost a decade after she died.
But the ITBP – which is funding the recovery operation – wants Morup's body to be returned by September, and is looking for mountain rescue Sherpa groups who could do the job.
Once returned to India, the body will undergo DNA testing and, if confirmed to be Morup, his remains will be given back to his family.
'My heart refused to believe he had died'
For years, Morup's family back in Ladakh have struggled to come to terms with his disappearance.
Now around 75, Yangskit struggles to recall even the day she was married. But the days after the tragedy remain etched in her mind.
"I only knew there was a storm on the mountain. Even though we organised cremation prayers at home, my heart refused to believe he had died," she says with tears rolling down her face.
"I didn't see his dead body, so it was difficult for me to believe it."
All that remains of Morup today are his medals and trophies, a couple of old photos from his mountain adventures – and, most importantly, a certificate from the Chinese government which states that at 17:30 on 10 May 1996, Morup reached the top of Everest.
If the recovery mission is successful, Morup's son Punchok Dorjai told the BBC that the family would hold a funeral for him near the Martyrs Park in Ladakh's capital Leh.
"My father gave his life for the country and he should be remembered as a martyr," Dorjai said, adding that his teammates who perished deserve the same title.
The family will also proudly save a symbol of Morup's legacy at their home, to go alongside his summit certification, he said: "We are planning to keep the Green Boots."
Additional reporting by Pradeep Bashyal, BBC News Nepali

title: Sophia Laforteza steps away from Katseye, the second member to depart this year
summary: The announcement came comes after fellow bandmate Manon Bannerman went on a hiatus from the ensemble.
full_text:
Sophia Laforteza steps away from Katseye, the second member to depart this year
- Published
Katseye vocalist Sophia Laforteza has announced she will temporarily step away from the popular girl group over mental health concerns.
The departure comes less than six months after fellow bandmate Manon Bannerman said she would go on hiatus from the ensemble, known for its global hits Gnarly, Pinky Up and Gabriela.
Laforteza "will be temporarily unable to participate in upcoming promotional activities", HYBE x Geffen Records said in a statement.
"We understand how much EYEKONS were looking forward to seeing Sophia on stage, but it is imperative that her mental health and wellness are prioritized," the label said of the Filipino-American superstar.
The label said Laforteza has been receiving "the utmost support" and consulting medical professionals, and has been advised to dedicate time to "extended rest and ongoing care to ensure a full recovery".
"While Sophia herself is eager to perform alongside her members, the health, safety, and long-term well-being of our artists will always remain our highest priority," the statement said, noting that her condition will be reassessed in September.
In a separate statement, Laforteza wrote on Instagram: "Making this decision wasn't easy, but I'm learning that health has to come first. I'm realizing that if I don't take care of my mind and body now, I won't be able to keep doing what I love the most for so long."
She added: "It means more to me than I could ever say. I promise I'm going to work as hard as I can to get through this, heal properly, and come back stronger."
The girl group formed with six members in 2023 and was nominated for two Grammy Awards last year. It now will continue events with four members.
The group has previously said its members have received multiple online death threats since they made their debut.
In February, the label announced that Katseye member Bannerman would take a temporary break to focus on her health and wellbeing, as well. She has not returned but their label has said the door will always be open.
The 23-year-old Swiss singer told fans she was "healthy" and "taking care of myself".
The group said the decision had been made following "open and thoughtful conversations together".
